lessons.title: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost
lessons.objective: Explain scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, the scale of preference and the production possibility frontier.

content.heading: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
paragraphs: Every economy starts from the same mismatch: wants are unlimited, but the resources used to satisfy them are limited. Economics studies how people and societies choose among competing uses.

content.heading: Wants, scarcity and choice
paragraphs: A student with N5,000 wants a new textbook, a data bundle and a pair of shoes. She can afford only one, so she ranks them and buys the textbook.

Wants are unlimited while the resources that satisfy them — land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship — are limited. That gap is scarcity. Scarcity is not the same as a shortage: scarcity is the permanent gap between wants and resources, while a shortage is a temporary shortfall in supply.

Because resources are scarce, every person, firm and government must choose. A scale of preference ranks wants from most to least pressing, and a rational choice compares the benefit of an option with its cost before deciding.
bullets: Wants are unlimited; resources are limited.
Scarcity is permanent and relative; a shortage is temporary.
A scale of preference ranks wants; rational choice weighs benefit against cost.
content.takeaway: Scarcity forces choice; a shortage only interrupts supply.

check.question: A fuel queue that disappears once tankers deliver is best described as ______.
check.why: The gap was temporary and supply fixed it; scarcity is the permanent gap between wants and resources.

visual.caption: Scarcity forces a choice, and every choice carries an opportunity cost.

content.heading: Opportunity cost and the basic questions
paragraphs: A state government has N40 billion and must choose between a new road and a new hospital. If it builds the road, the hospital is the alternative it gives up.

Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made, not the money paid. The N40 billion is the money cost; the hospital is the opportunity cost. Only the highest-ranked alternative forgone counts, not every option that was rejected.

Production creates goods and services, distribution shares them among people and places, and consumption uses them. Every society answers three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. Efficient resource use means producing what people value at the least cost, without waste.
bullets: Opportunity cost is the forgone alternative, not the money spent.
Production creates, distribution shares, consumption uses.
What, how and for whom are the three basic questions.
Efficiency means no wasted resources.
content.takeaway: The real cost of a choice is the best alternative you gave up.

check.question: A farmer plants maize instead of cassava on his land. His opportunity cost is ______.
options: the cost of the maize seed
the cassava he did not plant
check.why: The next best use of the land was cassava; seed and revenue are money flows, not the alternative forgone.

content.heading: The production possibility frontier
paragraphs: An economy can produce tanks or tractors, and every extra tank costs some tractors. The production possibility frontier draws that trade-off as a curve.

The PPF shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. A point on the curve is efficient, a point inside means resources are idle or wasted, and a point outside is unattainable until resources or technology grow.

The slope of the curve is the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other. It steepens as more of a good is produced because resources are not equally suited to both uses. Better technology or more resources shifts the whole curve outward.
bullets: On the curve: efficient. Inside: idle resources. Outside: unattainable.
The slope measures opportunity cost.
Growth shifts the curve outward.
content.takeaway: The PPF is scarcity drawn as a boundary and choice drawn as a move along it.

check.question: A point inside a country's production possibility curve indicates ______.
check.why: The economy could produce more of at least one good without giving up the other, so some resources are idle.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Opportunity cost is the alternative forgone, not the naira paid. If N2,000 buys data instead of a textbook, the opportunity cost is the textbook, not the N2,000.

content.problem: A student has N2,000 and ranks a textbook first, a data bundle second and a cinema ticket third. She buys the textbook. State her opportunity cost and explain why the N2,000 is not it.

steps.reason: Opportunity cost is measured against what was actually chosen.
steps.predictPrompt: Which want ranked next?

steps.reason: Only the highest-ranked forgone option counts, not every option skipped.
steps.result: The data bundle is the next best alternative.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.operation: Separate money cost from opportunity cost
steps.reason: The N2,000 is what she paid, not what she gave up.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: A state government with a fixed budget must choose between a new road and a new hospital. Explain its opportunity cost and show how the choice can be illustrated on a production possibility curve.
hints: Name the next best alternative, not the money spent.
On a PPF, the two goods are the axes and a movement along the curve is the trade-off.
A point inside the curve would mean the budget is not fully used.

content.heading: Go deeper: The money you spend is not the cost you bear
paragraphs: Explicit cost is the money that actually leaves your pocket, such as school fees, transport fares or the price of a textbook. Economic cost is wider: it is explicit cost plus the value of the best alternative you gave up to make the same choice.

This is why a free place at a crowded event is rarely free. The ticket may cost nothing, but the afternoon spent travelling and queueing could have been spent studying or selling goods. The alternative you surrendered is part of the economic cost.

Accountants count only money costs and call the remainder profit, while economists also count the normal reward the owner could have earned elsewhere. A trader who earns nothing in money terms may still be making an economic loss because her time and capital could have earned a return in another trade.

In examinations, the trap is to treat the receipt as the answer. Whenever a question mentions money paid, ask first what the person surrendered in order to pay it, because that surrendered alternative is what the economist records.
bullets: Money paid is explicit cost; the forgone alternative is economic cost.
Time, effort and lost earnings count as economic costs even when no cash changes hands.
Accounting profit can be positive while economic profit is negative.

content.heading: Go deeper: Reading a production possibility frontier like an examiner
paragraphs: A frontier is a boundary with two faces. Points on it use all resources properly, points inside waste resources, and points outside describe output the economy cannot yet reach. Most examination errors come from treating a point inside as just another efficient point.

Movement along the frontier shows reallocation: more schooling means less housing, not because resources have grown but because they have been switched. A shift of the whole frontier means something different, because the economy can now produce more of both goods.

A shift outward follows improved technology, newly discovered resources, better skills or more capital equipment. A shift inward follows war, flood, disease or an exodus of skilled workers. The same direction logic applies to every frontier question.

Nigerian examples make the test vivid. A poorly run power supply that leaves factories idle pushes an economy inside its frontier, while rural electrification and better seeds can move it outward without any change in the shape of the curve itself.
bullets: Inside means idle resources; on the curve means full use; outside means unattainable.
A move along the curve is reallocation; a shift is growth or decline.
Technology, resources, skills and calamity shift the frontier; prices alone do not.

content.heading: Go deeper: When choice disappears and when it only pretends to
paragraphs: Not everything scarce is produced, and not everything produced is scarce. Air is wanted but cannot be produced, so its price is zero and it creates no choice. Scarcity in economics means an unlimited want meeting a limited means, not simply that a good is expensive.

A good can be free and still scarce once people realise that access takes time and effort. A public park charges no entry fee, yet the space, quiet and parking spots there are limited. The moment rivalry appears, choice and rationing reappear with it.

There is also the edge case of a good that is abundant in one season and scarce in another. Mangoes may be cheap during harvest and dear months later. The scarcity itself has not changed, but the shortage has, since scarcity describes the permanent gap and shortage the temporary pressure.

Recognise the limit of the theory as well. Choice explains what people sacrifice, but it does not tell them that the sacrifice is fair or that the ranking is wise. A rational chooser can still choose badly, which is why economics describes the logic of choice rather than blessing every outcome.
bullets: Air is wanted but not produced, so scarcity without production is possible.
A free good becomes an economic good once access is rival and limited.
Seasonal abundance changes the shortage, not the underlying scarcity.

lessons.title: Economic Systems
lessons.objective: Compare free enterprise, centrally planned and mixed economies, and explain how Nigeria's mixed economy answers the basic questions.

content.heading: Economic systems
paragraphs: Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom. The institutions that answer those questions define its economic system.

content.heading: Three systems, three answers
paragraphs: A city allocates land by price, a ministry allocates it by quota, and a mixed system does both. Each is answering the same three questions differently.

An economic system is the set of institutions and rules a society uses to allocate scarce resources. Free enterprise relies on private ownership and the price mechanism; a centrally planned economy relies on state ownership and a plan; a mixed economy uses both.
The systems differ in who owns the factors of production, who takes decisions and what motivates producers. Ownership, coordination and incentive are the three tests to apply in an exam.
bullets: Free enterprise: private owners, prices, profit.
Centrally planned: state owners, plan, quotas.
Mixed: markets plus government.
content.takeaway: An economic system is defined by who owns, who decides and what motivates.

check.question: In a free enterprise economy, the three basic questions are answered mainly by ______.
check.why: Private owners respond to prices and profit, so prices coordinate what is produced, how and for whom.

content.heading: Free enterprise and central planning
paragraphs: A private firm opens a factory because it expects profit, while a ministry opens one because the plan requires it. That difference in motivation shapes how each system performs.

Free enterprise gives private individuals ownership, lets prices coordinate decisions and rewards efficiency with profit. Its merits are consumer choice, competition and rapid response to demand; its weaknesses are inequality, monopoly and neglect of public goods.

A centrally planned economy gives the state ownership and directs resources through a plan. It can mobilise resources for national goals and reduce inequality, but it often suffers from poor information, shortages and weak incentives.
bullets: Free enterprise: choice, competition, profit; inequality and monopoly.
Planned: national goals and equity; shortages and weak incentives.
Price signals versus plan targets.
content.takeaway: Markets coordinate through prices; plans coordinate through targets.

check.question: Which is a merit of a centrally planned economy?
options: rapid mobilisation of resources for national goals
check.why: A plan can direct resources to a national goal quickly; the other options describe market strengths.

visual.caption: The systems differ in ownership, coordination, incentive and main weakness.

content.heading: The mixed economy in Nigeria
paragraphs: A Nigerian household buys petrol from a private station, sends children to a public school and pays a regulated electricity bill. The same economy contains markets and government direction.

A mixed economy combines private ownership with public provision and regulation. Nigeria is mixed: private firms dominate production and trade, while government provides defence, roads and schools, regulates utilities and manages the oil sector.

Contemporary reforms show the mix shifting: deregulation of telecoms and the downstream oil sector, the 2005 banking consolidation that raised the minimum capital of banks, and cash policy reforms intended to reduce the cost of handling physical cash.
bullets: Nigeria: private production, public provision and regulation.
Reforms: deregulation, banking consolidation, cash policy.
The mix changes with policy, not with the textbook label.
content.takeaway: A mixed economy is a balance, and Nigerian reforms keep moving that balance.

check.question: Nigeria's economy is best described as ______.
check.why: Private firms produce most goods while government provides public goods, regulates and intervenes in key sectors.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not call Nigeria capitalist or socialist. It is mixed — private firms produce most goods while government provides public goods, regulates and intervenes in key sectors.

content.problem: Classify each decision: (a) a ministry sets a production quota for state farms; (b) a private firm raises output because prices rose; (c) the government provides roads while private firms run the buses.

steps.reason: State ownership plus a production quota is direction by plan.
steps.predictPrompt: What signal drives the private firm in (b)?

steps.reason: A private firm responding to a price rise is following the market signal.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: Public provision of roads alongside private production of bus services combines both sectors.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: Nigeria deregulated the downstream oil sector. Explain how that reform changes the balance between market and state, and name one benefit and one risk.
hints: Deregulation removes a controlled price and lets private importers and marketers set prices.
A benefit is supply that responds to price; a risk is volatility or weak protection for poor consumers.
Link the answer back to the three questions: what, how and for whom.

content.heading: Go deeper: How prices coordinate without anyone in charge
paragraphs: The price system works because it compresses information. A trader in a Kano market does not need to know why yam harvests failed in another state; the higher price arriving from the market already tells her that yams are now scarcer and worth more to grow, store or sell.

Each participant only follows a local signal yet the result is coordinated. When prices fall, producers cut output and buyers take more; when prices rise, the reverse happens. No committee meets to decide these moves, because the price itself carries the decision.

This decentralised knowledge is the deepest virtue of a market system. Local conditions, weather, tastes and skills are known best by the people who live with them, and prices let that scattered knowledge guide production without being collected in one place first.

The mechanism has a blind spot, however. Prices only signal what buyers pay for, so goods nobody can pay for, such as care for the destitute, send no signal at all. That silence is why most real systems correct the market rather than leaving prices alone.
bullets: A price is a compressed message about scarcity, not just a payment.
Decentralised decisions aggregate into coordination without a central plan.
Markets cannot signal needs that buyers cannot afford to express.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why central plans struggle with information and incentives
paragraphs: A planner must gather the same knowledge that prices carry, but through reports rather than signals. Reports travel slowly, arrive in bundles, and are shaped by whoever writes them, so the plan is often deciding on last month's facts while the market has already moved on.

The incentive problem follows. A manager rewarded for meeting a quota has reason to produce the target amount with the worst acceptable quality. A farmer who must surrender the harvest has little reason to try new seeds. Shortages and poor quality are therefore symptoms of the system, not accidents within it.

Planners also face a measurement difficulty. In a market, waste shows up as loss; under a plan, waste can hide inside inflated cost figures because nobody who bears the loss is checking independently. The numbers in the plan look exact while the economy behind them is not.

The fairness of the planning idea should not be confused with the performance of planning. Directing resources to a school or a hospital achieves equity quickly. The examination point is narrower: targets can command quantity, but they struggle to command the information and effort that make quantity desirable.
bullets: Plans move on reported data; markets move on price signals.
Quotas reward meeting the target, not exceeding it well.
Waste hides more easily where nobody bears the loss.

content.heading: Go deeper: Where Nigeria's mixed economy draws its boundary
paragraphs: A mixed economy is not half capitalist and half socialist in equal measure; it is a market economy with corrections. Nigeria's private sector produces food, clothing, transport and phones, while government keeps the armed forces, the courts, the currency and the trunk roads largely in public hands.

Deregulation moves the boundary in one direction and regulation moves it back. When a formerly state-run service is opened to private operators, prices become market-set and entry becomes competitive. When government imposes safety, labour or environmental rules on private firms, it is still correcting the market, not planning production.

The examination trap is to read the label instead of the institution. A private hospital selling operations in a market is free enterprise; a free public clinic funded from taxes is public provision; a private clinic inspected and licensed by government shows both logics in one building. Classify by the mechanism, not the label.

Public goods explain much of the boundary. Defence, street lighting and disease surveillance are hard to sell by the unit, so taxes fund them. The market handles goods that can be priced, while the state handles those that cannot, and Nigerian policy is the running argument about where one side stops and the other begins.
bullets: Private production plus public provision is the normal mixed-economy pattern.
Deregulation hands a decision to the market; regulation corrects it.
Classify by the mechanism in play, not by the name of the firm.

lessons.title: Methods and Tools of Economic Analysis
lessons.objective: Distinguish inductive from deductive reasoning and positive from normative statements, and use tables, charts, averages and dispersion to read economic data.

content.heading: Methods and tools of economic analysis
paragraphs: Economics uses reasoning to build explanations and statistical tools to describe data. The method and the measure both shape the conclusion.

content.heading: Induction, deduction and two kinds of claim
paragraphs: An economist notices that fuel prices rose in six states and concludes that they rose nationwide. Another starts from the theory that higher costs raise prices and predicts the same result.

Inductive reasoning moves from particular observations to a general conclusion. It is useful for spotting patterns but risks a hasty generalisation. Deductive reasoning moves from a general premise to a particular prediction; it is only as good as the premise.

A positive statement can be tested against evidence, such as 'removing the subsidy raised pump prices'. A normative statement expresses a value judgement, such as 'government should keep the subsidy'. Positive is not the same as true; it means testable.
bullets: Induction: particular to general. Deduction: general to particular.
Positive statements are testable; normative statements are value judgements.
Test the premise before trusting a deduction.
content.takeaway: Positive claims can be checked; normative claims can only be argued.

check.question: 'The government should spend more on education' is a ______ statement.
check.why: It recommends what ought to be done, so it is a value judgement rather than a testable claim about what is.

content.heading: Tables, charts and graphs
paragraphs: A trader records monthly maize prices in a table, then plots them on a line graph to see the trend. The table holds detail; the graph shows shape.

A table arranges data in rows and columns. A chart presents the same data visually — a bar chart compares categories, a pie chart shows proportions of a whole, and a line graph shows change over time. A graph plots the relationship between two variables, such as price and quantity.
These tools reveal trends and comparisons quickly, but they can mislead. A truncated axis exaggerates a small change, a poorly chosen chart hides variation, and a graph without units cannot be read.
bullets: Table: detail. Bar: categories. Pie: proportions. Line: time.
A graph shows how two variables move together.
Check the scale, the units and the starting point.
content.takeaway: A chart is only as honest as its scale and its units.

check.question: A pie chart is most useful for showing ______.
options: the relationship between price and quantity
check.why: Each slice is a share of the whole, so a pie chart shows proportions; a line graph is better for time and a scatter or curve for a relationship.

content.heading: Averages and spread
paragraphs: Two classes both average 60 marks, but one has marks from 58 to 62 and the other from 20 to 100. The average alone hides that difference.

The mean adds all values and divides by their number; the median is the middle value when the data is ordered; the mode is the most frequent value. The mean uses every value but is pulled by extremes, the median resists outliers, and the mode is best for the most common category.

Dispersion measures how spread out the data is. The range is the highest value minus the lowest; variance and standard deviation measure how far values sit from the mean, and the standard deviation uses the same units as the data. The range is quick but ignores the middle values, while the standard deviation uses every value.
bullets: Mean: all values. Median: middle. Mode: most frequent.
Outliers pull the mean, not the median.
Range is quick; standard deviation uses every value.
content.takeaway: An average describes the centre; dispersion describes how much the centre hides.

check.question: A shoe shop wants the size most customers ask for. The best measure is the ______.
check.why: The mode identifies the most frequent value, which is the size to stock in the largest quantity.

visual.caption: The mean uses every value; the median resists an extreme one.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A positive statement is not automatically correct — it is one that can be tested. 'Fuel prices rose' is positive; 'fuel prices are too high' is normative.

content.problem: A trader's daily sales are 4, 6, 6, 8 and 11 bags. Find the mean, median, mode and range.

steps.reason: The median needs the values in order before the middle can be located.
steps.predictPrompt: Which value appears most often?

steps.reason: Add every value and divide by the number of values.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the question tell you to find first?

steps.reason: The median is the third of five ordered values; the mode is the most frequent.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: The range is the highest value minus the lowest.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: A report says average income rose by 20 per cent, but most workers say they feel poorer. Explain how the mean and the median can tell different stories, and what measure of spread would help.
hints: A few very high incomes pull the mean above the income of most workers.
The median is the middle income, so it is not moved by the top earners.
A measure of spread shows whether incomes are clustered or widely unequal.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why two movements together do not prove one caused the other
paragraphs: Correlation only says that two series move together; causation says one moves because of the other. Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together in summer, yet nobody believes ice cream causes drowning. The hidden factor is the hot weather that raises both.

Economists hunt for such confounders before they claim cause. A rise in fuel prices followed by a rise in food prices looks like proof, but the true driver may be a general inflation affecting both markets at once. Without controlling for that third force, the sequence misleads.

Timing adds another guard. A cause must come before its effect, so a training programme that starts after sales have already risen cannot claim the rise as its result. Reversed timing is a common descriptive error in reports that read a chart backwards.

The safe exam habit is to ask what else changed. If a third factor plausibly moves both variables, the data shows association only, and any causal claim needs either a theory that explains the link or evidence that rules the third factor out.
bullets: Correlation shows movement together; causation shows movement because of.
A third factor can raise two series at once.
The cause must precede the effect.

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing the average that does not lie
paragraphs: The mean is the right average when values are fairly even and every value matters, such as total sales across many shops. It fails badly with extreme values, because a single very large sale lifts the mean above the experience of the typical shop.

The median is the right average when extremes would distort the picture, which is why house prices and incomes are often reported with the median. Half the values sit below it and half above, so one mansion cannot drag the typical house price upward.

The mode answers a different question altogether: which value occurs most often. It is the only average that can describe a category, such as shoe size, shirt colour or the most common occupation, and it is useless for continuous data where every value differs.

Averages also hide shape. Two datasets can share the same mean with entirely different distributions, one clustered tightly and the other spread widely. That is why the standard deviation or the range must travel with the average whenever the conclusion concerns variability.
bullets: Use the mean when values are even; the median when extremes skew the data.
Use the mode for the most frequent category, not for a typical amount.
Report spread alongside the average, or the comparison is incomplete.

content.heading: Go deeper: How honest data gets drawn dishonestly
paragraphs: A truncated axis is the commonest visual lie. If a chart of cement prices starts at a high value instead of zero, a small rise looks like a surge. The data is true, but the picture invites a conclusion the numbers cannot support.

Pie charts commit a different error: they show proportions beautifully and quantities badly. A slice holding two fifths of output looks similar to one holding three fifths, so a pie chart should never carry a claim about absolute amounts.

Bar and line charts can also mislead through poor categorisation. Grouping dissimilar goods into one bar, or connecting yearly points thathide seasonal swings, smooths away the very variation the analyst should have examined.

Sampling brings its own traps. A survey of one motor park cannot describe a whole state, and a question that leads respondents toward one answer manufactures the result it pretends to discover. Ask who was sampled, how many, and whether the wording steered the answer.
bullets: Check where the axis starts before believing the slope.
Pie charts show shares, not amounts.
Small or steered samples produce precise-looking errors.

lessons.title: The Theory of Demand
lessons.objective: Explain the law of demand, distinguish a movement along the curve from a shift, and compare the types and elasticity of demand.

content.heading: The theory of demand
paragraphs: Demand is not the same as a wish: it is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price. The law of demand and its exceptions organise every demand question.

content.heading: The law of demand
paragraphs: When tomato prices jump in the market, buyers take fewer tomatoes and some switch to okra. That everyday response is the law of demand at work.

The law states that, all other things equal, quantity demanded falls as price rises, so the demand curve slopes downward. A demand schedule lists quantity demanded at each price, and plotting it gives the demand curve.

Three reasons explain the slope: a higher price makes buyers substitute other goods, it reduces their real income, and each extra unit yields less satisfaction. Demand also depends on income, tastes, population, expectations and the prices of related goods.
bullets: Demand means willingness and ability to buy, not mere desire.
Quantity demanded falls as price rises, all else equal.
Income, tastes, population, expectations and related prices also matter.
content.takeaway: Demand is a schedule of willingness and ability, not a wish.

check.question: The law of demand states that, all else equal, ______.
options: quantity demanded rises as price rises
quantity demanded falls as price rises
check.why: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions along a demand curve, which is why it slopes downward.

content.heading: Movement along or shift of the curve
paragraphs: A bus fare rises and passengers take fewer trips; separately, a fuel price rise makes the same passengers avoid buses at every fare. The first is a movement along the curve, the second a shift.

A change in the good's own price moves the buyer along the demand curve, which is a change in quantity demanded. A change in income, tastes, population, expectations or the price of a related good shifts the whole curve, which is a change in demand.

For a normal good, demand rises with income; for an inferior good, demand falls as income rises. A rise in the price of a substitute shifts demand right, while a rise in the price of a complement shifts it left.
bullets: Own price: movement along the curve.
Any other determinant: shift of the curve.
Normal goods rise with income; inferior goods fall.
content.takeaway: Own price moves you along; every other determinant shifts the curve.

check.question: A rise in consumers' income shifts the demand curve for a normal good ______.
check.why: Income is not the good's own price, so the whole curve shifts; for a normal good, higher income raises demand at every price.

visual.caption: Own price moves you along the curve; every other determinant shifts it.

rows.right: Income, tastes, population or a related price

rows.left: Beans rise from N1,000 to N1,500
rows.right: A pay rise raises demand for rice

content.heading: Types of demand and elasticity
paragraphs: A torch is useless without a battery, palm oil serves both soap making and cooking, and the demand for bricklayers depends on the demand for houses. Those three cases are different types of demand.

Complementary or joint demand is for goods used together, such as a torch and its battery. Competitive demand is for substitutes, composite demand is one good with several uses, and derived demand is for a factor because of the good it produces.

Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity responds to price: percentage change in quantity divided by percentage change in price. Demand is elastic when the value exceeds one, inelastic when it is below one, and unitary when it equals one. Necessities with few substitutes, such as salt, are inelastic.
bullets: Complementary/joint, competitive, composite, derived.
PED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price.
Elastic above one, inelastic below one, unitary at one.
content.takeaway: Elasticity tells you whether a price change moves quantity a lot or a little.

check.question: The demand for bricklayers that arises from the demand for houses is ______ demand.
check.why: The factor is not wanted for itself but for the houses it helps to build, so its demand is derived from the product market.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A change in demand is not the same as a change in quantity demanded. If the question names the good's own price, stay on the curve; if it names anything else, shift it.

content.problem: The price of a good falls from N10 to N8 and quantity demanded rises from 100 to 140 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and interpret it.

steps.operation: Find the percentage change in quantity
steps.reason: Divide the change in quantity by the original quantity.
steps.predictPrompt: Now find the percentage change in price.

steps.operation: Find the percentage change in price
steps.reason: Divide the change in price by the original price, ignoring the sign.
steps.predictPrompt: Which numbers or terms work with each other first?

steps.reason: Elasticity is the quantity change divided by the price change.
steps.result: PED = 40 ÷ 20 = 2. Demand is elastic because the value exceeds one.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: A government wants to raise revenue by taxing cigarettes. Explain why the price elasticity of demand matters, and what would change if smokers could easily switch to a cheaper brand.
hints: If demand is inelastic, a tax raises price without cutting quantity much, so revenue rises.
Easy substitution makes demand more elastic, so buyers cut quantity sharply.
Link the answer to revenue, not only to health.

content.heading: Go deeper: The apparent exceptions to the law of demand
paragraphs: The law of demand is general because substitution, income effects and diminishing satisfaction almost always push quantity down as price rises. The exceptions are rare conditions where something else pushes harder in the opposite direction.

Giffen goods are the textbook case. They are inferior goods consumed by very poor households for whom the income effect dominates the substitution effect, so a higher price makes them poorer and forces them to buy even more of the inferior good.

Veblen goods travel the other way. Luxury items bought partly for display, such as conspicuous jewellery or designer labels, can face higher demand at a higher price because the price itself is part of the attraction. The buyer is purchasing status that cheaper versions cannot confer.

Examinations test whether you can name the mechanism, not just the label. If a good is inferior and the income effect is strong, Giffen logic applies; if it is conspicuous, Veblen logic applies; for nearly every ordinary good the downward slope remains the rule.
bullets: Giffen goods need a strong income effect on an inferior good.
Veblen goods benefit from a higher price because of display.
Nearly all ordinary goods still obey the downward slope.

content.heading: Go deeper: Normal and inferior goods at the income test
paragraphs: The normal and inferior distinction is a test of what income change does to demand. For a normal good, higher income raises demand at every price; for an inferior good, higher income lowers it, because buyers switch to a preferred alternative.

Inferior does not mean shoddy. Second-hand clothing, local grain substitutes or public transport can all be inferior in the technical sense while serving households well. The word describes the direction of the income effect, not the quality of the good.

Related goods give the sharpest exam discrimination. Substitutes such as rice and wheat or beef and fish move opposite to each other, while complements such as petrol and vehicles move together. A price rise shifts demand left for the complement and right for the substitute.

Expectations shift demand in a way students often miss. If buyers expect the price of beans to rise next month, they buy more today at every current price, which shifts demand right today even though today's price has not changed at all.
bullets: Normal goods rise with income; inferior goods fall with income.
Inferior describes the income effect, not poor quality.
Expected future prices can shift today's demand.

content.heading: Go deeper: What decides whether demand is elastic or not
paragraphs: A good with close substitutes faces elastic demand because buyers can leave easily. Salt and cooking oil have few substitutes and face inelastic demand, while a particular brand of biscuit faces elastic demand because the shelf next to it offers easy alternatives.

Necessity versus luxury works the same way. Insulin or basic food has no real substitute, but a holiday or a restaurant meal can be postponed or abandoned, so luxury demand stretches further when prices rise.

The share of the budget matters too. A price rise on a small item such as matches barely disturbs total spending, while a rise on school fees or rent claims a large share of income and forces a big behavioural change. Time also stretches elasticity, because habits and contracts adjust only gradually.

Market definition sets the ceiling. Demand for all food is inelastic, but demand for one brand of food is elastic, since the brand can lose buyers to rivals while food itself has nowhere to go. Always ask which market the question means before judging the number.
bullets: More substitutes mean more elastic demand.
Necessities and small budget shares are inelastic.
Narrower markets have more elastic demand than broad ones.

lessons.title: The Theory of Supply
lessons.objective: Explain the law of supply, distinguish a movement along the curve from a shift, and compare the types and elasticity of supply.

content.heading: The theory of supply
paragraphs: Supply is the quantity producers are willing and able to offer for sale at each price. The law of supply, its determinants and elasticity explain how sellers respond.

content.heading: The law of supply
paragraphs: When maize prices rise, farmers plant more maize and traders release more from storage. The higher price draws more supply into the market.

The law of supply states that, all other things equal, quantity supplied rises as price rises, so the supply curve slopes upward. A supply schedule lists quantity supplied at each price, and plotting it gives the supply curve.

The slope reflects rising opportunity cost: as producers expand, they use less suitable resources or pay overtime, so they need a higher price. Supply also depends on input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies, the number of sellers, expectations and weather.
bullets: Supply means willingness and ability to sell, not the stock in a warehouse.
Quantity supplied rises with price, all else equal.
Costs, technology, taxes, subsidies, sellers, expectations and weather shift supply.
content.takeaway: Supply is what sellers will actually offer, not what they happen to hold.

check.question: The law of supply states that, all else equal, ______.
options: quantity supplied rises as price rises
quantity supplied falls as price rises
check.why: Higher prices make extra production worthwhile, so quantity supplied and price move in the same direction.

content.heading: Movement along or shift of the curve
paragraphs: The market price of maize rises and farmers bring more to market; separately, a fall in the cost of fertiliser makes them supply more at every price. The first is a movement along the curve, the second a shift.

A change in the good's own price moves the seller along the supply curve, which is a change in quantity supplied. A change in input costs, technology, taxes, subsidies, the number of sellers, expectations or weather shifts the whole curve, which is a change in supply.
A fall in costs or a new technology shifts supply right, because more can be supplied at every price. A tax rise or a bad harvest shifts it left.
bullets: Own price: movement along the curve.
Any other determinant: shift of the curve.
Lower costs shift supply right; higher costs shift it left.
content.takeaway: Own price moves you along; every other determinant shifts the curve.

check.question: A fall in the cost of raw materials will ______.
options: shift the supply curve to the right
shift the supply curve to the left
move the seller along the supply curve
reduce quantity supplied at every price
check.why: Cheaper inputs raise the profit available at each price, so sellers offer more at every price and the curve shifts right.

visual.caption: Own price moves you along the curve; every other determinant shifts it.

rows.left: Maize rises from N300 to N400

content.heading: Types of supply and elasticity
paragraphs: A butcher sells beef and hides from the same animal, a farmer chooses between maize and cassava on the same land, and electricity reaches homes from hydro, gas and solar plants. Those cases are different types of supply.
Joint supply is produced together from one process; competitive supply uses the same resources for alternative products; composite supply comes from several sources for one market.

Price elasticity of supply measures the response of quantity supplied to price: percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price. Supply is elastic when producers can respond quickly, and inelastic when capacity, storage or time is limited. Time is the main determinant, which is why farm supply is inelastic within a season.
bullets: Joint: one process, several products.
Competitive: same resources, alternative products.
Composite: several sources, one market.
PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price.
content.takeaway: Supply is elastic when producers can respond, and time is the biggest constraint.

check.question: Beef and hides are produced together from the same animal, so their supply is ______.
check.why: One production process yields both goods, so an increase in beef supply also increases the supply of hides.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Do not confuse a movement along the supply curve with a shift. The good's own price moves you along; costs, technology, taxes and weather shift the curve.

content.problem: A supply function is P = ¼(Qs + 10). Find the quantity supplied when the price is N10.

steps.reason: The function gives price in terms of quantity, so isolate quantity before substituting.
steps.predictPrompt: What is 4P when P = 10?

steps.reason: Put P = 10 into the rearranged supply function.
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: The result is the quantity supplied at that price.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: Explain why the supply of tomatoes is inelastic within a single season but more elastic over two years.
hints: In one season, land, planting time and storage are fixed.
Over two years, farmers can plant more land, buy irrigation or build storage.
Link the time horizon to the elasticity coefficient, not just to output.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why more supply needs a higher price
paragraphs: The upward slope comes from rising opportunity cost. A farmer who has planted his best soil first must move to poorer plots or work longer hours to squeeze out extra bags, so each additional unit costs more than the one before it.

Firms hire workers in order of ability and rent space in order of suitability, so the cheapest inputs are used first. Expanding output means paying higher wages, overtime rates or rents, and only a higher price makes that extra cost worth bearing.

Capacity adds a second wall. A mill that runs on one shift can add a second and then a third, but each extra shift costs more in supervision, power and machine wear than the last. Beyond full capacity, expansion needs new buildings, which is a far larger price signal.

Stockpile release works differently and students often confuse the two. The law of supply concerns production decisions taken over time, while releasing stored stock responds instantly to price. A trader dumping inventory at a high price is reacting to stocks, not to the cost of producing more.
bullets: Expansion moves to less suitable resources first, so costs rise.
Overtime and extra shifts make capacity more expensive.
Releasing stock is not the same as producing more.

content.heading: Go deeper: Expectations and other quiet shifters of supply
paragraphs: Expectations shift supply in the opposite direction to demand, which traps many candidates. If sellers expect the price of yam to rise next month, they hold back stock today, shifting today's supply left even while the current price is unchanged. A fall in expected price does the reverse.

Input costs shift supply because they change the profit available at every price. Cheaper fertiliser lets a farmer profit from output that previously lost money, shifting supply right. A higher wage bill or a new transport levy does the opposite by raising the cost of every unit.

Technology shifts supply by widening the frontier of the possible. Improved seeds, irrigation or automated packing let the same resources produce more, so more is supplied at every price. A tax rise shifts supply left, while a per-unit subsidy shifts it right by the same logic.

Weather and the number of sellers complete the picture. A drought shifts food supply left because output falls at every price, and the entry of new sellers into a market shifts supply right. Either way, the curve moves because the conditions of supply changed, not the price.
bullets: Expected price rises shift current supply left; falls shift it right.
Input costs, technology, taxes and weather shift the curve.
More sellers at every price means a rightward shift.

content.heading: Go deeper: Time is the main governor of supply elasticity
paragraphs: In the market period, which lasts only days or weeks, output is already produced or already stored. Farmers cannot plant in response to a price rise, so supply is almost perfectly inelastic and price must do all the adjusting.

In the short run, producers can work overtime, run extra shifts or strain existing equipment. Supply responds a little, but capacity still binds, so elasticity grows only modestly. Storage gives traders slightly more room, yet perishable farm produce cannot be stored for long.

In the long run, producers can build new plants, clear new land, train workers and adopt new technology. Supply becomes elastic because the whole capacity of the firm or the market can be rearranged to meet a sustained price signal.

Perishability and storability set natural limits. Wheat can be carried over a season, but tomatoes cannot, which is why tomato prices swing violently within a season while grains move more gently. Always ask which time horizon the question assumes before judging the answer.
bullets: Market period: output is fixed, so supply barely responds.
Long run: capacity can be rebuilt, so supply responds freely.
Perishables are less elastic than storable goods over time.

lessons.title: The Theory of Price Determination
lessons.objective: Explain how market forces set equilibrium price and quantity, and how price legislation changes the outcome.

content.heading: The theory of price determination
paragraphs: Price is set where buyers and sellers agree. Demand and supply, the price system and government legislation explain why the agreed price is what it is.

content.heading: Market, price and the price system
paragraphs: A tomato glut in one week and a tomato shortage the next show the same market adjusting: the price falls when sellers cannot sell and rises when buyers cannot buy.

A market is any arrangement in which buyers and sellers exchange a good, not only a physical place. Price is the amount of money for which a good or service exchanges, and the price system is the network of prices across markets.

The price system performs four jobs: it signals scarcity, rations limited goods among buyers, allocates resources towards profitable uses, and rewards efficient producers. A price is therefore information as well as income.
bullets: Market: any buyer-seller arrangement, not just a building.
Price: money value of a good in exchange.
Price system: signals, rations, allocates, rewards.
content.takeaway: A price is a signal before it is a payment.

check.question: The price mechanism determines the prices of commodities through ______.
check.why: In a market system, the interaction of demand and supply sets price; legislation is an external intervention.

content.heading: Equilibrium, surplus and shortage
paragraphs: A trader prices a bag of rice at N60,000 and cannot sell; at N45,000 buyers queue. Between those prices is the level where the market clears.

Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so a surplus pushes price down. Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so a shortage pushes price up.
A rise in demand raises both equilibrium price and quantity; a rise in supply lowers equilibrium price and raises quantity. The size of each change depends on the elasticity of the two curves.
bullets: Equilibrium: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Surplus pushes price down; shortage pushes it up.
Demand up: price and quantity up. Supply up: price down, quantity up.
content.takeaway: The market clears where the two curves cross; surpluses and shortages are temporary pressures.

check.question: At a price above the equilibrium price, there is ______.
check.why: Sellers offer more than buyers will take at that price, so unsold stock accumulates until price falls.

visual.caption: The two imbalances push the price in opposite directions.

content.heading: Price legislation and equilibrium equations
paragraphs: A government caps the price of bread below the market level to protect consumers, and queues appear because demand now exceeds supply. That is the predictable result of a maximum price.

A maximum price, or price ceiling, is fixed below equilibrium and causes a shortage, rationing and black markets. A minimum price, or price floor, is fixed above equilibrium and causes a surplus, so government may buy the excess; the minimum wage and farm price supports are examples.
Equilibrium can also be found from simple linear equations. Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied, solve for price, then substitute the price back into either equation to get quantity.
bullets: Maximum price below equilibrium: shortage and black market.
Minimum price above equilibrium: surplus and government purchase.
Set Qd = Qs, solve for P, then substitute for Q.
content.takeaway: A price fixed away from equilibrium creates the imbalance the market would have cleared.

check.question: A maximum price fixed below the equilibrium price will cause ______.
check.why: At the lower price buyers want more than sellers will offer, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A maximum price protects buyers by keeping prices low; a minimum price protects sellers by keeping prices high. Do not reverse the two.

content.problem: Given Qd = 15 − 2P and Qs = 5 + 3P, find the equilibrium price and quantity.

steps.operation: Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied
steps.reason: At equilibrium the market clears, so Qd = Qs.
steps.predictPrompt: How do you collect the P terms on one side?

steps.reason: Subtract 5 from both sides and add 2P to both sides.
steps.predictPrompt: What do you substitute, into which formula?

steps.reason: Either equation gives the equilibrium quantity at P = 2.
steps.result: Qd = 15 − 2(2) = 11, and Qs = 5 + 3(2) = 11. Equilibrium is P = 2, Q = 11.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: A government fixes a maximum price for bread below the equilibrium price. Explain the effects on quantity, queues and the black market, and why the policy may still be popular.
hints: At the lower price, quantity demanded rises while quantity supplied falls.
Queues and a black market appear because some buyers will pay more than the legal price.
The policy is popular because the buyers who succeed pay less, even though supply shrinks.

content.heading: Go deeper: How surplus and shortage undo themselves
paragraphs: A surplus means sellers hold stock that buyers at that price will not take. To move it, they cut price, and the lower price chokes off new supply while coaxing out more demand. The market therefore walks down toward the point where the curve pair crosses.

A shortage works in mirror image. Buyers compete for less than they want, bidding price upward, and the higher price calls out more supply while discouraging some demand. Queues are the sign that the price has not yet done enough of this work.

The adjustment needs freely moving prices to work. Where sellers must charge the legal price, neither the markdown nor the bidding-up can happen, so the surplus rots in store or the queue lengthens instead. Rigid prices freeze the imbalance instead of healing it.

Markets also need time, because contracts, harvests and menus cannot be rewritten in a day. A sudden price rise may therefore leave a shortage visible for weeks even in a free market, not because the mechanism has failed but because it is still working through the earliest constraints.
bullets: A surplus pushes price down; a shortage pushes it up.
Free price movement is what lets the market clear.
Fixed prices freeze imbalances instead of curing them.

content.heading: Go deeper: Price ceilings, floors and the world they create
paragraphs: A ceiling below equilibrium feels kind and acts harshly. Sellers produce less because the legal price rarely covers rising costs, buyers queue because demand at that price exceeds supply, and part of the market moves underground where the same good sells for more.

Quality quietly deteriorates under a ceiling as well. A baker who cannot raise the price of bread may shrink the loaf or thin the filling, because the legal price binds the stated number while the true value slips. Rationing by coupon or by connection replaces rationing by price.

A floor above equilibrium creates the opposite scene. Sellers produce heavily because the guaranteed price rewards output, buyers stay away because the price is high, and the resulting surplus must go somewhere. Government purchase, storage or destruction are the usual exits.

Nigerian classrooms often discuss fuel and farm support in these terms. A farm price support guarantees output income and needs a buyer for the surplus; a minimum wage guarantees income and needs workable enforcement. Both policies help the protected group and both must answer for the surplus or the lost jobs that follow.
bullets: Ceilings create shortages, queues and black markets.
Floors create surpluses that government must absorb.
Quality cuts and rationing often replace price as the adjuster.

content.heading: Go deeper: Finding equilibrium carefully and not double counting
paragraphs: The algebra is one idea dressed in symbols. Equilibrium means the two quantities agree, so setting Qd equal to Qs and solving for P finds the one price at which surplus and shortage both vanish. Substituting that price back gives the quantity at which they vanish together.

Always check by substituting into the other equation. If the two quantities disagree, an arithmetic slip has occurred, because at the true equilibrium both equations describe the same market outcome. This thirty-second check catches most careless errors before they cost marks.

Simultaneous change is the advanced trap. If demand rises while supply rises too, quantity surely rises but price could go either way, because the two shifts pull price in opposite directions. The safe answer is the direction that both shifts agree on, with price left undetermined.

The slope of each function carries information students ignore. A steep demand function means buyers respond sluggishly to price, while a flat supply function means sellers respond strongly. The relative slopes decide whether a demand shift mostly raises price or mostly raises quantity.
bullets: Set Qd equal to Qs, solve for P, then verify in both equations.
When both curves shift, only the agreed direction is certain.
Relative slopes decide if price or quantity absorbs the shock.

lessons.title: The Theory of Production
lessons.objective: Explain the production function, relate total, average and marginal product under the law of variable proportions, and compare economies of scale with returns to scale.

content.heading: The theory of production
paragraphs: Production turns inputs into output, and how output responds when a firm adds another worker or another machine is the core of the theory of production.

content.heading: Production and the production function
paragraphs: A baker buys flour, hires a worker and rents an oven; the bread that comes out is production. A firm combines inputs in a deliberate process, and the result can be a good or a service.

Production is primary when it extracts raw materials, secondary when it manufactures or builds, and tertiary when it provides services such as transport, banking and teaching. A production function shows the maximum output obtainable from given inputs, written Q = f(L, K).

In the short run at least one input, usually capital, is fixed; in the long run every input can change. Returns to scale compare output with a proportional change in all inputs: increasing returns when output rises faster, constant when it rises at the same rate, and decreasing when it rises more slowly.
bullets: Primary extracts, secondary makes, tertiary serves.
Short run: one input fixed. Long run: all inputs variable.
Returns to scale use a proportional change in every input.
content.takeaway: The production function is the recipe that turns inputs into output.

check.question: When all inputs double and output more than doubles, the firm has ______.
check.why: Output grows faster than the proportional increase in inputs, which is increasing returns to scale.

content.heading: Total, average and marginal product
paragraphs: A farmer adds workers to a fixed plot of land and records the harvest. The first workers share the land and tools, later ones crowd the same plot, and the extra output from each new worker eventually shrinks.
Total product is the output from all units of the variable input. Average product is total product divided by the number of units, and marginal product is the extra output from one more unit.

The law of variable proportions says that as more of a variable input is added to a fixed input, marginal product first rises, then falls, and eventually becomes negative. Diminishing returns begins where marginal product starts to fall, even while total product is still rising. Total product peaks where marginal product is zero.
bullets: AP = TP ÷ L; MP = change in TP ÷ change in L.
MP rises, then falls, then turns negative.
TP peaks where MP = 0.
content.takeaway: Marginal product turns down before total product does.

check.question: Diminishing returns set in when ______.
check.why: The law starts at the point where each extra unit of the variable factor adds less output than the one before, while total output can still rise.

content.heading: Division of labour, scale and productivity
paragraphs: A tailor who makes a shirt alone hires specialists for cutting, sewing and finishing, and output per worker rises. Specialisation and larger scale both raise output, but each has a limit.
Division of labour breaks production into specialised tasks. It raises skill and speed and saves tools and time, but it can bring boredom, over-dependence and coordination costs.

Internal economies of scale are cost savings from the firm's own growth: technical, managerial, marketing, financial and risk-bearing. External economies come from the industry's growth, such as a skilled labour pool, specialised suppliers and better infrastructure.
Productivity is output per unit of input, and it rises with training, technology, health, motivation and management. Producer equilibrium is reached where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
bullets: Division of labour trades higher output for boredom and dependence.
Internal economies come from firm size; external from industry size.
Productivity is output per input; MR = MC at equilibrium.
content.takeaway: Scale and specialisation raise productivity until coordination costs set in.

check.question: A firm's own growth lowers its average cost through ______.
check.why: Internal economies arise from the firm's own expansion; external economies come from growth of the whole industry.

visual.caption: Internal economies come from the firm; external economies come from the industry.

rows.left: Technical, managerial, marketing and financial savings
rows.right: Skilled labour pool, specialised suppliers, better infrastructure

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Diminishing returns is a short-run law with at least one fixed factor. Returns to scale is a long-run idea with every factor changing. Do not use the two terms interchangeably.

content.problem: A farm has fixed land. With 1, 2, 3 and 4 workers, total output is 10, 25, 35 and 40 tonnes. Find the marginal and average product, and identify where diminishing returns set in.

steps.reason: Marginal product is the change in total output when one more worker is added.
steps.result: MP = 10, 15, 10 and 5 tonnes for workers 1 to 4.
steps.predictPrompt: Which is the first fall in marginal product?

steps.reason: Average product is total output divided by the number of workers.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: The law begins where marginal product turns downward.
steps.result: MP rises from 10 to 15, then falls to 10 at the third worker, so diminishing returns set in there even though total output rises to 35 tonnes.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: A firm doubles all its inputs and output rises from 100 to 240 units. Name the returns to scale, and explain why the law of diminishing returns does not apply to this change.
hints: Compare the percentage rise in output with the 100 per cent rise in inputs.
Diminishing returns needs at least one fixed factor.
Doubling every input is a long-run change, so returns to scale is the right tool.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why output first rises faster and then slower
paragraphs: Land does not change when a farmer hires another worker, so each extra pair of hands must share the same soil, tools and water. At first, workers specialise and idle time falls, so the extra output from another worker is large. As more workers crowd the same plot, they wait for tools, trample seedlings and duplicate one another's tasks, so each addition contributes less than the one before.

Marginal product records that extra output, average product spreads total output across every worker, and total product equals accumulated marginal product. Average product rises while the newest worker adds more than the current average, and falls once the newest worker adds less than that average.

The law of variable proportions describes three phases of that crowding. In the first phase, marginal product rises because the fixed factor is fully utilised. In the second phase, marginal product falls but stays positive, so total output still grows more slowly. In the third phase, marginal product becomes negative and total output falls because congestion actively destroys output.

A common exam trap is to treat any slowing of growth as falling output. Diminishing returns begins when marginal product starts to decline, yet total product keeps rising until marginal product reaches zero. Only after that point does the harvest itself shrink.
bullets: Marginal product first rises with better utilisation, then falls with crowding.
Average product rises while marginal product exceeds it and falls after.
Total product peaks where marginal product reaches zero.
Diminishing returns means slower growth, not yet falling output.

content.heading: Go deeper: Specialisation, scale and the point where coordination bites
paragraphs: Specialisation raises output through four quiet channels. Workers learn by doing and repeat the same operation, machines can be designed for one task, idle time between jobs shrinks, and supervisors can balance workloads around known skills. A tailor who assigns cutting, stitching and finishing to different assistants exploits all four channels, which is why output per worker can rise even when the number of workers barely changes.

Internal economies of scale follow from a single firm's larger size rather than from a wider industry. A larger plant can use indivisible equipment that a small shop cannot justify, redeploy managers who only handle one function, negotiate cheaper inputs and spread the cost of advertising across more units. Each saving lowers average cost because the same capability serves a bigger output.

External economies arrive when neighbouring firms grow together. A cluster of furniture makers in an industrial area attracts sawmills, timber dealers and repair workshops, so each firm borrows the other's skills and suppliers without paying for them directly. Shared roads, ports and power connections work in a similar way by reducing the cost every firm must earn on its own.

Both forces have a stopping point. Excessive subdivision creates boredom, inspection costs and disputes about who is responsible when a defect appears, while very large firms need more management layers and slower decisions. When those coordination costs outweigh the savings from specialisation and scale, average cost rises again and productivity falls.
bullets: Specialisation saves time, improves skill and justifies specialised tools.
Internal economies come from one firm's growth; external economies from industry growth.
Coordination costs eventually offset savings from scale and subdivision.

content.heading: Go deeper: Short-run crowding versus long-run scaling
paragraphs: The law of variable proportions answers a short-run question: what happens when one input changes while another stays fixed. Because land, factory space or machinery cannot adjust immediately, the variable input eventually meets a bottleneck and its marginal contribution declines. The fixed factor is the hidden constraint in every calculation.

Returns to scale answers a different question: what happens when every input changes in the same proportion. Doubling workers, machines and floor space together removes the bottleneck that produced diminishing returns, so there is no reason for proportional crowding to appear. The experiment therefore isolates whether the technology itself favours large operation.

Increasing returns to scale means a balanced expansion more than doubles output, often because specialised teams and indivisible equipment become worthwhile. Constant returns means output doubles exactly, while decreasing returns means output rises less than proportionally, usually because management and communication become harder across a wider operation. The distinction matters when a firm chooses between many small plants and one large plant.

Productivity is the bridge between the two ideas. Returns to scale describe the shape of the production function, while productivity measures how much output each input actually yields in practice. A firm can enjoy increasing returns on paper yet record low productivity if workers are idle, materials arrive late or supervisors lack training, so the exam answer should separate technology from performance.
bullets: Variable proportions vary one input against a fixed factor.
Returns to scale vary all inputs together in one proportion.
Decreasing returns signal coordination diseconomies, not crowding of one input.

lessons.title: Theory of Costs and Revenue
lessons.objective: Distinguish fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, compare accountants' and economists' notions of cost, and relate revenue concepts to the firm's supply decision.

content.heading: Theory of costs and revenue
paragraphs: A firm's costs and revenue decide whether it stays in business, and each cost measure answers a different question about production.

content.heading: Fixed, variable and total cost
paragraphs: A bakery pays rent whether it bakes one loaf or a thousand, but flour and casual wages rise with every loaf. The first cost is fixed and the second is variable.
Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run: rent, insurance, administrative salaries and machinery. Variable costs change with output: flour, fuel, packaging and hourly labour.

Total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost. Average fixed cost is fixed cost divided by output and falls continuously as output rises; average variable cost is variable cost divided by output; average total cost is total cost divided by output. Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit, and it cuts average total cost at the lowest point of the average cost curve.
bullets: TC = TFC + TVC.
AFC = TFC ÷ Q; AVC = TVC ÷ Q; ATC = TC ÷ Q.
MC = change in TC ÷ change in Q.
content.takeaway: Fixed costs are paid for existing; variable costs are paid for producing.

check.question: Rent and administrative expenses are examples of ______.
check.why: They are paid whether or not output is produced, so they do not vary with the quantity made.

visual.caption: The two costs respond to output in opposite ways.

rows.right: Average variable cost falls, then rises

content.heading: Short-run and long-run costs
paragraphs: A transport company cannot buy new buses this month, but over five years it can expand its fleet. The short run fixes the fleet; the long run lets the firm choose it.

In the short run at least one factor is fixed, so the firm has fixed and variable costs. In the long run all factors can change, so every cost is variable and the firm picks the plant size that minimises cost at each output.

Short-run average cost is U-shaped because average fixed cost falls while diminishing returns eventually raise average variable cost. The long-run average cost curve is the envelope of the short-run curves: it falls with economies of scale and rises with diseconomies of scale. Accountants count only explicit costs, the money paid out; economists add implicit costs, the opportunity cost of the owner's resources.
bullets: Short run: fixed and variable. Long run: all variable.
Long-run AC is the envelope of short-run curves.
Economic cost = explicit + implicit cost.
content.takeaway: Accountants count money paid; economists also count what was given up.

check.question: An economist's cost differs from an accountant's cost because it includes ______.
check.why: The economist adds the opportunity cost of resources the owner supplies, which the accountant does not record as a payment.

content.heading: Revenue and the firm's supply decision
paragraphs: A pure water seller gets N20 a sachet and sells 500 sachets a day, so total revenue is N10,000. Revenue is not the same as profit, because the costs of sachets, water and labour still have to be paid.

Total revenue is price times quantity. Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price in perfect competition. Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit.

In perfect competition the firm is a price taker, so average revenue and marginal revenue both equal price. A firm with market power faces a downward-sloping demand curve and must lower price to sell more, so marginal revenue is below price. A firm maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and the marginal cost curve above average variable cost is its short-run supply curve.
bullets: TR = P × Q; AR = TR ÷ Q = P.
Perfect competition: AR = MR = P.
Profit-maximising output: MR = MC.
content.takeaway: A competitive firm supplies where price equals marginal cost.

check.question: A perfectly competitive firm's marginal revenue is ______.
check.why: The firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so each extra unit adds exactly the price to total revenue.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Accounting profit ignores implicit costs. A business can report an accounting profit while making an economic loss once the owner's forgone salary and capital are counted.

content.problem: A firm has fixed cost of N120,000 and variable cost of N2,000 per unit. Find total cost, average total cost and marginal cost at 60 units.

steps.reason: Variable cost per unit times the number of units gives total variable cost.
steps.predictPrompt: What is total cost once fixed cost is added?

steps.reason: Total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost.
steps.predictPrompt: In your own words, why does this step come before the next one?

steps.reason: Average total cost is total cost divided by output; marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit.
steps.result: ATC = N240,000 ÷ 60 = N4,000. MC = N2,000, because each extra unit adds only its variable cost.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: A firm has fixed costs of N100,000 and variable costs of N30 per unit. It sells at N50. Find the break-even quantity and explain why the marginal cost curve above average variable cost is its supply curve.
hints: At break-even, total revenue equals total cost.
Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost.
The firm supplies only when price covers average variable cost, and output is set where price equals marginal cost.

content.heading: Go deeper: The U-shape of average cost and marginal cost
paragraphs: Two forces pull average total cost in opposite directions as output grows. Fixed cost is spread over more units, so average fixed cost falls quickly at first and then more slowly, while variable cost per unit eventually rises when overtime and diminishing returns set in. Average total cost is the sum of those two schedules, and its U-shape records which force dominates at each output.

Marginal cost is the extra cost of the next unit, driven mainly by variable input prices and the productivity of the added input. While marginal cost lies below average total cost, the new unit costs less than the current average, so the average is pulled down. Once marginal cost climbs above average total cost, each unit pulls the average upward instead.

The two curves therefore meet at the lowest point of average total cost, by arithmetic rather than convention. A Nigerian baker who adds a second oven inherits a larger fixed cost that must be spread, yet the new oven removes a bottleneck that had raised marginal cost. The same logic explains why a transport firm accepts a low fare for spare seats: the extra passenger adds little cost.

In the long run the firm chooses plant size first, so it traces the envelope formed by the lowest points of each short-run average cost curve. That envelope falls while economies of scale dominate and rises when diseconomies such as congestion dominate. The short-run curve shows the plant already owned; the long-run curve shows the plant it would select for each output.
bullets: Average fixed cost falls as fixed cost spreads.
Marginal cost pulls average total cost down below it and up above it.
The long-run average cost curve is the envelope of short-run curves.

content.heading: Go deeper: Money paid out versus opportunity forgone
paragraphs: Explicit costs are observable cash outflows such as rent, wages, flour and fuel. Implicit costs never reach the ledger but still represent resources withdrawn from their next best use: the owner's unpaid labour, a shop owned by the family, or capital saved in the business instead of placed in a savings account. Economic cost adds the two together because profit must beat every alternative, not only the bank statement.

Normal profit is the return an owner needs to keep resources in a business rather than move them elsewhere. A kiosk operator who earns accounting profit but less than the salary offered in a formal job may be losing money in economic terms. The test is therefore comparative: would those same hours, premises and funds earn more elsewhere, and by how much?

The distinction changes entry and exit decisions. An entrepreneur will enter a new trade only when expected revenue covers explicit costs, implicit costs and a normal return, and will leave when it persistently fails to do so. That is why a firm can report a small accounting surplus while still shrinking in economic terms, as the owner gradually withdraws unpaid time and capital.

An exam trap is to list normal profit alongside rent and wages as if it were a third bill. Normal profit is a part of the opportunity cost of ownership, not a payment made to a supplier. Counting it twice either overstates costs or misstates the point at which a business becomes uneconomic, which is exactly the error the question is designed to expose.
bullets: Economic cost is explicit cash plus implicit opportunity cost.
Normal profit is the minimum return to retaining resources in a trade.
Accounting profit above zero can still mean an economic loss.

content.heading: Go deeper: When price takers meet price makers
paragraphs: A price taker sells one more unit without changing the price, so the extra revenue equals the price. A price maker must lower the price slightly to sell more, and that reduction applies to every unit already sold, not only to the new one. Marginal revenue is therefore less than price, and the gap widens where demand is less responsive to price.

Profit rises with any unit whose marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost and falls after the gap closes. The firm expands until marginal revenue equals marginal cost because the last unit adds as much to revenue as to cost. Producing beyond that equality adds more to cost than to revenue and erodes profit, while producing less leaves profitable units unsold.

The same equality anchors the short-run supply curve. At any price below minimum average variable cost, marginal revenue cannot cover the extra cost of producing, so the firm withholds supply until price recovers. Above that floor, each price calls forth the quantity where marginal cost equals that price, which traces the rising segment of the marginal cost curve.

Nigerian illustrations make the contrast concrete.
