A sachet-water seller near a bus park faces many substitutes and cannot raise price without losing every customer, so extra revenue tracks the posted price. A cement brand with few rivals and loyal builders can hold price on existing orders while discounting only new contracts, so its marginal revenue sits visibly below the headline price.
bullets: For price makers, marginal revenue equals price minus the loss on existing units.
Output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost exhausts profitable units.
Short-run supply follows marginal cost above minimum average variable cost.

lessons.title: Factors of Production and Their Rewards
lessons.objective: Identify the four factors of production and their rewards, explain how wages, interest and profit are determined, and relate mobility and efficiency to unemployment.

content.heading: Factors of production and their rewards
paragraphs: A rice farm uses land, hired workers, a tractor and a manager who takes the risk of the harvest. Those four inputs are the factors of production, and each is paid differently.

content.heading: The four factors and their features
paragraphs: Land covers all natural resources, including soil, water, minerals and forests. Its supply is fixed, it is geographically immobile and its reward is rent.

Labour is human effort, physical or mental. It is inseparable from the worker, perishable if unused and varies in skill, and its reward is wages or salaries. Capital is man-made producer goods such as machines, tools and buildings; it is produced, depreciates and earns interest.

Entrepreneurship organises the other factors, innovates and bears the risk of loss. Its reward is profit, which is a residual: what remains after the other factors are paid, and it can be negative. Factor mobility is the ease of moving a factor to another use or place; land is immobile, while labour and capital are more mobile.
bullets: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit.
Land is fixed and immobile; labour is mobile but perishable.
Profit is residual and can be negative.
content.takeaway: Each factor is paid for its role, and only the entrepreneur carries the residual risk.

check.question: The reward for capital as a factor of production is ______.
check.why: Capital is man-made producer goods, and the payment for its use is interest; rent is for land and profit is the entrepreneur's residual.

content.heading: Wages, interest and profit
paragraphs: A hospital pays radiographers more than cleaners because few workers can read scans, and a lender charges interest for giving up cash today. Scarcity of skill and time both shape factor payments.

The marginal productivity theory of wages says a worker is paid the value of the extra output produced. Demand for labour is derived from demand for the product and slopes downward; supply depends on population, training, alternatives and working conditions.

Interest is the reward for parting with liquidity, according to the liquidity preference theory. People demand money for transactions, precaution and speculation, and the interest rate adjusts to balance that demand with the money supply. Profit rewards risk-bearing, uncertainty and innovation, and it is the residual left after other costs.
bullets: Wage = value of marginal product in the theory.
Interest balances liquidity preference with the money supply.
Profit is the residual reward for risk and innovation.
content.takeaway: Wages follow productivity, interest follows liquidity, and profit follows risk.

check.question: The liquidity preference theory explains the determination of ______.
check.why: The theory says the interest rate balances the demand for money to hold as liquidity against the supply of money.

visual.caption: A scarce skill raises the value of the marginal product, and with it the wage.

steps.label: Scarce skill
steps.detail: Few workers can do the task

content.heading: Mobility, efficiency and unemployment
paragraphs: A welder moves from Kano to Lagos for higher pay, while a clerk whose job is automated cannot move into software work. Mobility and skill decide who can reach the jobs that exist.

Occupational mobility is the ease of moving between jobs; geographical mobility is the ease of moving between places. Housing, family ties, skills and information affect both, and low mobility keeps wage differences alive.
Labour efficiency is output per worker. It rises with education, training, health, technology, motivation and good management, and it falls with poor working conditions.

Unemployment has several forms: frictional unemployment is the search between jobs, structural unemployment is a mismatch of skills, seasonal unemployment follows the calendar, and cyclical unemployment follows a downturn. Solutions include skills training, infrastructure, diversification and support for small firms.
bullets: Occupational mobility: between jobs. Geographical: between places.
Efficiency rises with training, health, technology and management.
Match the type: frictional, structural, seasonal, cyclical.
content.takeaway: Mobility and skills decide whether a worker can reach the job that exists.

check.question: A farmer who has no work between harvests is ______ unemployed.
check.why: The work disappears on a predictable calendar pattern, which is seasonal unemployment, not a skills mismatch or a downturn.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Profit is a residual, not a cost. Do not list it with rent, wages and interest when asked for the rewards of the factors of production.

content.problem: A firm employs 10 workers who produce 200 units sold at N50 each. The last worker adds 15 units. Find the value of the marginal product and state the highest wage the firm can pay that worker.

steps.reason: The last worker's extra output is given as 15 units.
steps.predictPrompt: What is each extra unit worth?

steps.reason: Multiply the extra output by the price of the product.
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: The firm will not pay more than the value the worker adds.
steps.result: The highest wage is N750; at a lower wage the firm can profitably hire more workers.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: Explain why a radiographer may earn more than a cleaner using the marginal productivity theory, and name two factors that could weaken the theory.
hints: Compare the value of the extra output each worker produces.
Training and licensing limit the supply of radiographers.
Wages can also be set by unions, minimum-wage law or discrimination, not productivity alone.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why land, labour and capital move differently
paragraphs: Land is fixed in aggregate and cannot move between places, so its reward adjusts through rent rather than migration. A plot near a busy market earns more because traders value its position, not because the soil itself travels. Mineral deposits, forests and water bodies share that locational character even when mining or irrigation changes how intensively they are used.

Labour moves with its owner but perishes when unused. A trained mason who spends a month without work loses both income and practice, while the same worker can carry skill from Kano to Lagos if housing and family arrangements allow. Skill mismatch then becomes the binding barrier: the carpenter may relocate easily yet remain unable to take the software job that pays more.

Capital is man-made and can be accumulated, but its mobility depends on its form. Money can switch industries quickly, while a specialised mould, a dam or a highway cannot. Depreciation erodes that capital over time, so the stock must be maintained or replaced. The reward therefore reflects both the wait to commit resources and the risk that a particular asset becomes obsolete.

Entrepreneurship cannot be stored or shipped at all. It exists only when a person judges markets, organises teams and accepts uncertainty about the outcome. That limits its supply to individuals rather than to purchases, which explains why imaginative organisers can command large residual gains in one venture and bear losses in the next.
bullets: Land is immobile and earns scarcity rent from location and fertility.
Labour is mobile with the worker but perishable and skill-specific.
Capital is producible and depreciates; entrepreneurship is non-storable judgement.

content.heading: Go deeper: Liquidity preference in a cash-heavy economy
paragraphs: People hold money to spend soon, to guard against surprises and to wait for better opportunities. Transactions balances cover daily purchases, precautionary balances absorb a sudden school fee or repair bill, and speculative balances wait for an asset price to fall. Together these motives form the demand for money, which every holder balances against the return from holding interest-bearing assets.

Interest is compensation for parting with liquidity. A trader who keeps cash in a lockbox avoids bank charges and can pay instantly, but gives up the interest that a deposit would earn. When interest rates rise, the cost of holding idle cash increases, so some balances shift into deposits or treasury instruments until the convenience of readiness equals the forgone return.

Liquidity preference describes that shifting rather than a fixed pile of cash. In a cash-heavy setting such as informal trade, many sellers prefer physical notes because customers pay in cash and transfers may face delay or limits. Their demand for money is therefore stubborn, while digital balances sit closer to the speculative margin where the interest rate exerts stronger influence.

The theory does not claim that interest alone sets wages or prices. It explains one market, the market for money, where demand meets the supply controlled by the central bank and by bank lending. An exam trap is to treat every motive as speculative, when in fact only the wait-for-opportunity motive responds directly to expected asset prices.
bullets: Transactions and precautionary balances serve planned and unexpected spending.
Speculative balances wait for cheaper assets and respond to expected returns.
Interest compensates holders for surrendering immediate liquidity.

content.heading: Go deeper: What marginal productivity leaves out
paragraphs: Marginal productivity theory predicts pay from a simple chain: a worker adds output, that output is sold, and the firm hires until the added value equals the wage. The argument assumes the firm can adjust employment freely, workers are close substitutes, and output prices are known. Where those conditions hold, persistent wage gaps track genuine differences in added value.

Many labour markets violate those assumptions. A dominant employer in a town can pay below added value because quitting is costly, a legal minimum wage can hold pay above short-run marginal product, and collective agreements can raise pay for retention rather than for immediate output. Discrimination, transport costs and family responsibilities also keep equally productive workers in differently paid jobs.

Informal work in Nigeria sharpens the problem. Casual labour, piece-rate tailoring and street trading rarely produce a clean marginal product that a firm compares with a posted wage. Output fluctuates with customer flow, weather and credit from suppliers, so pay reflects bargaining power and access to trading space as much as any measured addition to production.

Efficiency wages add a further twist: pay above the market clearing level can raise output through motivation, lower turnover and better health. That predicts wages exceeding marginal product in the short run without implying permanent exploitation. A strong answer names the conditions under which the theory works and the institutional factors that push actual pay away from its prediction.
bullets: The theory requires free hiring, substitutable workers and observable output.
Monopsony, minimum wages and bargaining shift pay from marginal product.
Informal and piece-rate work obscure any clean marginal product.

lessons.title: Market Structures
lessons.objective: Compare perfect competition with monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly, and apply break-even and shut-down analysis.

content.heading: Market structures
paragraphs: Markets differ in how much power a seller has, and that power decides price, output and whether a firm survives.

content.heading: Perfect competition
paragraphs: A grain market with hundreds of traders selling identical maize is the closest real example of perfect competition. No trader can ask more than the market price without losing every buyer.

Perfect competition rests on many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect information and perfect factor mobility. Each firm is so small that it cannot influence price, so it is a price taker with a horizontal demand curve.

The firm's average revenue equals marginal revenue equals price. In the short run it maximises profit where marginal cost equals marginal revenue and can earn supernormal profit or a loss. In the long run, free entry and exit remove both, so firms earn only normal profit and produce at the minimum of long-run average cost.
bullets: Many sellers, identical product, free entry, perfect information.
Price taker: AR = MR = P, so demand is horizontal.
Short run: MC = MR. Long run: normal profit at minimum LAC.
content.takeaway: Perfect competition is a benchmark where no firm can move the market price.

check.question: A perfectly competitive firm's demand curve is ______.
check.why: The firm can sell any quantity at the market price but nothing above it, so its demand curve is horizontal.

content.heading: Imperfect markets
paragraphs: A telecoms firm sets its own tariff, a cement oligopoly watches rivals' prices, and a noodle maker differentiates its brand. Each has some power over price.
An imperfect market has firms that can influence price because products are differentiated or sellers are few. The firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve and is a price maker.

A pure monopoly has one seller, no close substitute and high barriers to entry; it maximises profit where MR = MC and may practise price discrimination, charging different buyers different prices for the same good. Monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products with easy entry, so short-run supernormal profit attracts entrants and long-run profit falls to normal. An oligopoly has a few large interdependent firms that compete through advertising, branding and service rather than price.
bullets: Monopoly: one seller, barriers, price maker, MR = MC.
Price discrimination needs market power, separated markets and no resale.
Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, easy entry.
Oligopoly: few firms, interdependence, non-price competition.
content.takeaway: Market power rises as sellers become fewer and products become more distinct.

check.question: A market with many sellers of differentiated products and easy entry is ______.
check.why: Differentiated products give each seller some price power, while easy entry keeps long-run profit at normal.

visual.caption: The two ends of the market-power spectrum.

content.heading: Break-even and shut-down
paragraphs: A bus company keeps running during a fuel spike while fares still cover fuel and drivers' daily pay, but stops when fares cannot cover even those variable costs.
A firm breaks even when total revenue equals total cost, so it earns normal profit. Break-even occurs where average revenue equals average total cost.

The shut-down point is the minimum of average variable cost. If price falls below it, the firm cannot cover its variable costs and loses less by stopping production in the short run, because fixed costs are paid either way.
A firm that shuts down still pays fixed costs, so its short-run loss equals fixed cost. It exits only in the long run, when all costs become variable.
bullets: Break-even: TR = TC, or AR = ATC; normal profit.
Shut-down: price below minimum AVC.
At shut-down the short-run loss equals fixed cost; exit is a long-run decision.
content.takeaway: A firm can survive a loss but not a price below average variable cost.

check.question: A firm should shut down in the short run when price falls below ______.
check.why: Below minimum average variable cost, revenue cannot cover the cost of producing at all, so stopping limits the loss to fixed cost.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Break-even and shut-down are not the same. Breaking even means normal profit; shutting down means production stops because price cannot cover variable cost.

content.problem: A firm sells at N50. At its current output, average total cost is N60 and average variable cost is N45. Should it shut down in the short run, and what is its loss per unit?

steps.operation: Compare price with average variable cost
steps.reason: The shut-down test asks whether revenue covers the cost of producing at all.
steps.result: N50 is above N45, so the firm should keep producing in the short run.
steps.predictPrompt: How much does each unit contribute to fixed cost?

steps.reason: Price minus average variable cost is the amount each unit adds towards fixed cost.
steps.result: Contribution = N50 − N45 = N5 per unit.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: Average total cost exceeds price, so the firm makes a loss on each unit.
steps.result: Loss = N60 − N50 = N10 per unit, but shutting down would lose the average fixed cost of N15 per unit.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: A monopoly and a perfectly competitive firm both face a fall in demand. Explain how their price and output responses differ, and which is more likely to shut down in the short run.
hints: The competitive firm is a price taker and cannot hold price above the market level.
The monopolist chooses output where MR = MC and may keep price higher by restricting output.
Compare price with minimum average variable cost in each case.

content.heading: Go deeper: How a monopolist can charge different prices
paragraphs: Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices for the same good or service, and it needs three conditions working together. The seller must possess market power so buyers cannot simply turn to a rival, buyers must be separable into groups with different willingness to pay, and resale must be hard to police. Without that separation, a discounted ticket returns to the market and destroys the higher price.

The simplest form approximates perfect discrimination by negotiating separately with each buyer, pushing price towards individual valuation. The second form offers a menu, such as blocks of electricity or bundles of data, where heavier users choose larger blocks at a lower average price. The third form uses observable group markers, such as student or off-peak status, to offer a lower price without asking each buyer to reveal valuation.

Nigerian illustrations show the menu logic even without direct price data. A telecom operator sells smaller data bundles at a higher unit price and larger bundles at a lower unit price, letting heavy users self-select. A transport company may discount off-peak seats because an empty seat earns nothing, while passengers who must travel at peak hours pay more for the same journey.

The limits matter for exams. Discrimination fails when identity can be disguised, when a low-price buyer can resell to a high-price buyer, or when regulation requires uniform tariffs. It can also feel unfair when essential services are involved, which is why regulators sometimes outlaw group pricing even if it would raise revenue.
bullets: Discrimination requires market power, separable buyers and blocked resale.
Menus let buyers self-select; group markers use observable characteristics.
Arbitrage and uniform-tariff rules are the main constraints.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why entry erodes profit in monopolistic competition
paragraphs: Monopolistic competition begins with differentiated products that customers perceive as distinct, so each firm initially faces a downward-sloping demand curve. If that firm earns more than normal profit, outsiders notice the margin and enter with similar varieties. Entry does not merely split existing sales; it shifts each incumbent's demand curve left because customers now have another place to go.

As demand drifts inward, the price the firm can charge for any output falls. The firm contracts along its marginal cost curve until demand becomes tangent to long-run average cost, capturing normal profit and no more. Product differentiation softens competition but does not protect profit in the long run when entry remains free and brands cannot block imitation.

Nigerian soap, biscuit and noodle brands illustrate the cycle. A new flavour or package earns attention and a temporary premium, rivals watch sales rather than list prices, and advertising responds faster than price cuts. Once shelf space fills, each brand must spend more to defend loyalty, which raises cost while demand keeps shrinking towards the tangency point.

Oligopoly behaves differently because few rivals make entry unlikely and retaliation credible. A monopolist blocks entry altogether, while a perfect competitor never has profit to defend. Confusing those cases is the core exam trap: monopolistic competition predicts long-run normal profit precisely because entry is easy, not because products are identical.
bullets: Differentiation creates temporary pricing power under free entry.
Entry shifts incumbent demand inward until normal profit alone remains.
Easy entry distinguishes monopolistic competition from oligopoly and monopoly.

content.heading: Go deeper: Contribution, sunk costs and the shutdown test
paragraphs: Contribution is the amount each sale contributes towards fixed costs after variable costs are covered. Price minus average variable cost gives contribution per unit, and total contribution across all units must be compared with fixed costs to judge the short-run position. A positive contribution means continuing to produce loses less than stopping, even when total revenue falls short of total cost.

Consider a hypothetical service selling at a price above variable cost but below total cost. Each trip still adds cash that helps cover rent, licences and permanent staff, so shutting down would forfeit that contribution while fixed bills remain. That arithmetic explains why a bus operator endures a fuel spike: as long as fares cover fuel, drivers and tolls, the route survives a temporary loss.

Fixed costs in the short run are sunk in the sense that they must be paid whether buses run or stand idle. The shutdown comparison therefore asks which loss is smaller: fixed cost when closed, or fixed cost minus contribution when open. The firm shuts only when price drops below minimum average variable cost and contribution turns negative.

The long run reverses the test because every cost becomes avoidable. A firm that cannot cover total cost over time must exit, sell assets or redeploy capital. Exams often conflate the two horizons by applying the break-even rule to the short run; the break-even point uses total cost, while the shutdown point uses variable cost alone.
bullets: Contribution per unit is price minus average variable cost.
Continue in the short run while contribution covers part of fixed cost.
Exit in the long run when revenue cannot cover total cost.

lessons.title: Money and Inflation
lessons.objective: Explain the functions and qualities of money, apply the quantity theory to the price level, and distinguish the causes, effects and control of inflation and deflation.

content.heading: Money and inflation
paragraphs: Money makes exchange possible without barter, and inflation decides how much that money can actually buy.

content.heading: Functions, qualities and supply of money
paragraphs: A trader who once swapped yams for cloth now accepts naira because every seller will take it. General acceptability, not the paper itself, makes money useful.

Money is anything generally accepted as a means of payment, and it removes the double coincidence of wants that makes barter difficult. Its functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.

Its qualities are general acceptability, divisibility, portability, durability, homogeneity and limited supply. The demand for money comes from transactions, precaution and speculation. The supply of money is currency in circulation plus bank deposits; the central bank controls the monetary base while banks create deposits through lending.
bullets: Functions: exchange, unit of account, store of value, deferred payment.
Qualities: acceptable, divisible, portable, durable, homogeneous, scarce.
Demand motives: transactions, precaution, speculation.
Money supply: currency plus bank deposits.
content.takeaway: Money works because everyone accepts it, not because it is valuable in itself.

check.question: The function of money that allows goods to be valued and compared is ______.
check.why: Prices are quoted in money, so it acts as a common unit for comparing the worth of different goods.

content.heading: Quantity theory and the value of money
paragraphs: When too much naira chases the same quantity of goods, each naira buys less. That is the quantity theory in everyday form.

The quantity theory of money states MV = PT: the money supply times its velocity equals the price level times the volume of transactions. If velocity and output are constant, a rise in the money supply raises the price level.

The value of money is its purchasing power, the quantity of goods one unit can buy. It moves inversely with the price level: when prices double, the value of money halves. Inflation is measured with a consumer price index: a base year is chosen, a basket of goods is priced, and the index is the current basket cost divided by the base-year cost times 100.
bullets: MV = PT.
Value of money = 1 ÷ price level.
CPI = current basket ÷ base basket × 100.
content.takeaway: More money chasing the same output lowers what each unit of money can buy.

check.question: If the price level doubles, the value of money ______.
check.why: Purchasing power is the inverse of the price level, so doubling prices halves what each unit can buy.

content.heading: Inflation, deflation and control
paragraphs: A fixed-salary teacher finds her pay buys less each term, while a debtor finds his loan easier to repay. Inflation redistributes income between them.

Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level. Demand-pull inflation comes from excess aggregate demand; cost-push inflation comes from rising input costs; imported inflation enters through higher import prices. Stagflation is inflation coexisting with high unemployment.

Inflation hurts fixed-income earners, savers and creditors, while borrowers gain because they repay in cheaper money. Deflation is a persistent fall in the price level; it helps those on fixed incomes but can delay spending and raise real debt.

Control uses monetary policy, fiscal policy, income policy such as a wage freeze, and supply-side measures that raise output. Deflation is fought with lower interest rates, public spending and credit expansion.
bullets: Demand-pull, cost-push, imported, stagflation.
Inflation hurts savers and creditors; deflation can raise real debt.
Control: monetary, fiscal, income and supply-side policy.
content.takeaway: Inflation is controlled by reducing demand or raising supply, not by blaming one price.

check.question: A wage freeze is a policy measure aimed at ______.
check.why: A wage freeze is an income policy that slows cost-push pressure by limiting the growth of wages and prices.

visual.caption: Demand-pull starts with buyers; cost-push starts with sellers' costs.

rows.right: Input costs such as fuel and wages rise

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Inflation is a rise in the general price level, not the price of one item. A single expensive bag of rice is not inflation.

content.problem: A basket of goods cost N20,000 in the base year and N25,000 this year. Calculate the consumer price index and the inflation rate.

steps.reason: Divide the current basket cost by the base-year cost and multiply by 100.
steps.predictPrompt: What does an index of 125 mean?

steps.reason: The base year has an index of 100, so 125 means prices are 25 per cent higher.
steps.result: The basket now costs 125 per cent of its base-year price.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: Inflation is the percentage change in the index from the base year.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.question: Government prints money to pay salaries while output is unchanged. Use MV = PT to explain the effect on prices and the value of money, and name one group that gains and one that loses.
hints: With velocity and output fixed, a rise in M must raise P.
A higher price level means a lower value of money.
Borrowers gain and fixed-income earners lose when prices rise.

content.heading: Go deeper: How lending can expand deposits
paragraphs: A bank that lends does not simply pass along a pile of cash. When it approves a loan, it credits the borrower's deposit account and simultaneously records a loan asset against that deposit liability. The deposit is newly created money in the borrower's hands, available for spending, transfer or saving. Lending therefore expands the deposit component of the money supply without waiting for physical notes to arrive.

The textbook multiplier then follows the chain of re-deposits. The borrower spends, the recipient deposits at another bank, that bank lends a fraction of the new deposit, and the process continues until cash leaks out or ratios change. The mechanical total equals the initial reserve divided by the required reserve ratio, which is why textbooks present a large potential expansion.

Real expansion falls short of that arithmetic for ordinary reasons. Borrowers hold extra cash for security, banks keep excess reserves when creditworthy demand is weak, and customers shift balances between banks or into other assets. Cash leakage is especially strong where informal trade settles in notes, so each round of re-deposit loses a larger share than the ratio alone predicts.

The central bank anchors the process through the monetary base of currency plus bank reserves. It cannot create broad money directly, but by changing reserve conditions and the price of borrowing it influences how far the banking system stretches each unit of base. An exam trap is to picture banks lending out deposits one-for-one; the correct picture is loans creating deposits, constrained by reserves and demand for credit.
bullets: Bank loans create deposits by crediting the borrower's account.
The multiplier is a potential ceiling, not a guaranteed outcome.
Cash leakage, excess reserves and weak credit demand limit expansion.

content.heading: Go deeper: Baskets, base years and why inflation is measured
paragraphs: Inflation is measured by pricing a fixed basket of goods and services in a base year and in the current year. The consumer price index divides the current basket cost by the base-year cost and multiplies by one hundred, so a value above one hundred records cumulative growth since the base. The result depends on which items enter the basket and how heavily each one weighs.

Weights reflect household spending, which is why food, transport, rent and fuel dominate a typical Nigerian index. A rise in palm oil prices therefore moves the index far more than a rise in an item bought rarely, even if both jumps look similar. National statisticians revise weights as consumption patterns change, but they retain the basket between revisions so that price change can be compared cleanly.

The index is not a perfect record of lived cost. Households substitute towards cheaper foods or change brands, while the fixed basket still assumes the old choice. That substitution bias overstates inflation, while quality change can push the measure in the other direction. Both effects explain why personal experience may diverge from the headline figure.

The value of money is the reciprocal of the price level, so moderate inflation quietly transfers wealth from savers and creditors to debtors. The exam discrimination is between a single price jump and a general rise: one item soaring raises the index only by its weight, whereas inflation requires broad cumulative growth across the basket.
bullets: The index compares a weighted basket with its base-year cost.
Heavily weighted items such as food move the index most.
Substitution and quality change make the index imperfect but consistent.

content.heading: Go deeper: Stagflation and the trade-off in control
paragraphs: Stagflation combines high inflation with high unemployment because supply shocks raise costs without raising demand. A fuel price jump lifts transport and food costs, while weaker trading conditions cut hiring at the same time. Textbook demand management assumes inflation and unemployment move opposite each other, so stagflation exposes the limit of that simple trade-off.

Monetary tightening cools excess demand by raising borrowing costs, but it cannot lower the price of imported fuel or repair a broken supply chain. Fiscal spending supports jobs yet adds to demand, which worsens demand-pull pressure if output is constrained. Policy must therefore ask whether the inflation originates in spending, in costs or in the exchange rate before choosing an instrument.

Nigeria's import dependence makes imported inflation distinctive. A softer currency raises the naira cost of fuel, machinery and wheat, which then lifts domestic prices through transport and production margins. Controlling that channel requires supply-side measures as well as interest rates: reliable power, ports and storage raise output so that demand growth meets more goods rather than higher prices.

Expectations prolong every episode. Once workers demand compensating pay rises and traders pre-emptively raise prices, cost-push pressure feeds itself even after the original shock fades. Credible policy therefore combines a clear interest-rate stance with measures that expand supply, so that disinflation does not have to be purchased entirely with lost jobs.
bullets: Stagflation pairs cost-driven inflation with weak employment.
Demand tools misfire when the shock is imported or supply-driven.
Expectations can turn a shock into persistent inflation.

lessons.title: International Trade and Comparative Advantage
lessons.objective: Explain absolute and comparative advantage, interpret the terms of trade and the balances, describe Nigeria's trade and correction measures, and explain exchange-rate types and determination.

content.heading: International trade
paragraphs: Nigeria sells crude oil and buys refined fuel, machines and wheat. That exchange, and the rate at which it happens, is international trade.

content.heading: Basis for international trade
paragraphs: A country may be better at making everything, yet still gain from trade. The reason is opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Nigeria has oil but imports refined products, so it trades even with the raw resource.

Absolute advantage means producing more of a good with the same resources. Comparative advantage means producing it at a lower opportunity cost, and David Ricardo showed that specialising where opportunity cost is lowest raises total output even for a country that is better at everything.

Other gains are economies of scale, wider consumer choice, access to goods a country cannot produce and the transfer of technology. The terms of trade decide how those gains are shared, and a country whose export prices fall relative to import prices loses even when it trades more.
bullets: Absolute: more output per resource.
Comparative: lower opportunity cost.
Gains: scale, choice, technology.
content.takeaway: Trade pays because opportunity cost differs, not because one country is weaker.

check.question: The principle of comparative cost advantage was propounded by ______.
check.why: Ricardo showed that specialisation by comparative opportunity cost raises total output even when one country has an absolute advantage in everything.

visual.caption: Absolute advantage compares output; comparative advantage compares opportunity cost.

rows.left: More output from the same resources

rows.right: The real basis of beneficial trade

rows.left: One farm yields more cocoa per hectare
rows.right: A country gives up less coffee to grow cocoa

content.heading: Terms of trade, balances and Nigeria's trade
paragraphs: Nigeria exports mainly crude oil and imports refined fuel, machinery, food and manufactures. A fall in oil prices therefore worsens its terms of trade.

The terms of trade are the index of export prices divided by the index of import prices times 100; a rise means exports buy more imports. The balance of trade counts visible goods only, while the balance of payments adds services, income and transfers.

Invisible trade covers banking, shipping, insurance and tourism, and a goods deficit can be closed by remittances or capital inflows. Payments deficits are corrected by devaluation, tariffs, quotas, import substitution, export promotion and borrowing. A quota limits imports to a fixed quantity and dumping is selling abroad below home cost.
bullets: Terms of trade = export prices ÷ import prices × 100.
Trade balance: goods only; payments: everything.
Correction: devaluation, tariffs, quotas, export promotion.
The Nigeria Export Promotion Council supports exporters.
content.takeaway: A trade deficit is not a payments deficit, because services and transfers also move money.

check.question: The formula (index of export prices ÷ index of import prices) × 100 is used to measure the ______.
check.why: The ratio compares export and import prices, so it measures the commodity terms of trade, or how much imports a unit of exports can buy.

content.heading: Exchange rates
paragraphs: A traveller changes naira for dollars and finds the rate has moved since last month. The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. When the naira falls, imported fuel costs more and bus fares rise.
A fixed rate is pegged by the central bank, a floating rate is set by demand and supply, and a managed float combines both. Multiple rates apply different prices to different transactions.

The rate is determined by demand for and supply of foreign exchange, which depend on exports, imports, capital flows, inflation, interest rates and speculation. Devaluation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, which can correct a deficit but also raises domestic prices; revaluation does the opposite.
bullets: Fixed, floating and managed float.
Demand and supply set the rate.
Devaluation: cheaper exports, dearer imports.
content.takeaway: The exchange rate is a price, and like any price it moves with demand and supply.

check.question: Devaluation of a currency means ______.
options: a deliberate reduction in its value against other currencies
an increase in its value against other currencies
fixing its value permanently to gold
allowing it to float without any central-bank action
check.why: Devaluation lowers the official value of a currency, which makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A trade deficit is not the same as a payments deficit. Services, remittances and capital inflows can close a goods gap.

content.problem: With the same resources, Country A can produce 10 tonnes of cocoa or 5 tonnes of coffee; Country B can produce 4 tonnes of cocoa or 8 tonnes of coffee. Who should produce which?

steps.reason: Giving up 10 cocoa frees resources for 5 coffee, so 1 coffee costs 2 cocoa.
steps.result: A: 1 coffee = 2 cocoa, or 1 cocoa = 0.5 coffee.
steps.predictPrompt: Now do the same for B.

steps.reason: Giving up 4 cocoa frees resources for 8 coffee, so 1 coffee costs 0.5 cocoa.
steps.result: B: 1 coffee = 0.5 cocoa, or 1 cocoa = 2 coffee.
steps.predictPrompt: What information do you compare before deciding?

steps.reason: Each country should produce the good for which it gives up less.
steps.result: A has the lower cocoa cost (0.5 coffee vs 2), so A produces cocoa; B has the lower coffee cost (0.5 cocoa vs 2), so B produces coffee.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Explain how a fall in oil prices affects Nigeria's terms of trade and balance of payments, and name one policy response.
hints: Export prices fall while import prices change little, so the terms of trade worsen.
Export earnings fall, leaving a wider current-account deficit.
A response could be devaluation, export diversification or expenditure reduction.

content.heading: Go deeper: Specialisation when one country leads everything
paragraphs: Suppose two regions share the same resources but differ in skill mix. Region A can produce more of both groundnuts and cassava than Region B with the same inputs, yet its advantage is larger in one product than in the other. Trade still pays because what matters is the relative sacrifice of forgoing one good for the other, not the absolute pile of output.

The opportunity-cost calculation makes that sacrifice explicit. If Region A gives up less groundnut to make a unit of cassava, while Region B gives up less cassava to make a unit of groundnut, each specialises where its sacrifice is smaller. Combined production then exceeds what either region could achieve alone, and exchange can leave both better supplied than any self-sufficient allocation.

That logic extends beyond two goods. A country with abundant land, a deep port or cheap labour specialises in goods that use its plenty intensively, while importing what its scarce resources produce dearly. Nigeria's concentration on crude oil illustrates the cost of specialisation as well as its gain: export earnings grow, but dependence on one price makes income volatile when that price falls.

Terms of trade decide how the extra output is shared. If Nigeria's export prices fall while the price of imported food and machinery stays firm, the same volume of oil buys fewer imports and the gain from trade shrinks. Specialisation therefore needs a second question: is the country selling into a falling market while buying into a steady one?
bullets: Absolute advantage is irrelevant; relative opportunity cost governs specialisation.
Each region should produce where its sacrifice is lowest.
Terms of trade determine what share of extra output is retained.

content.heading: Go deeper: Goods, services and transfers in the payments balance
paragraphs: The trade balance records goods only, while the balance of payments records every transaction with the rest of the world. Current-account items include merchandise, services, primary income such as wages and investment earnings, and secondary income such as remittances and grants. A deficit on goods can therefore sit alongside a surplus on transfers without any accounting error.

Invisible trade covers banking, shipping, insurance, tourism and professional services. A Nigerian student paying fees abroad, a foreign auditor working in Lagos or a ship calling at a Nigerian port each creates a service payment that never passes through the customs ledger for goods. Measuring only vessels and warehouses thus understates the full external position.

Remittances support many households directly and stabilise the payments balance when merchandise is weak. They arrive as secondary income, finance school fees, food and small trading capital, and relieve pressure on export earnings. They do not, however, correct a structural goods deficit by themselves, because they depend on diaspora employment rather than on domestic production.

Deficits are closed through several channels with different side effects. Devaluation makes exports cheaper, tariffs and quotas restrict imports, export promotion expands foreign sales, and borrowing or foreign investment finances the gap temporarily. An exam trap is to treat correction as costless; each method shifts the burden onto exporters, consumers or future taxpayers.
bullets: Trade balance counts goods; payments balance counts goods, services, income and transfers.
Invisible items include banking, shipping, insurance and tourism services.
Remittances are secondary income, not merchandise exports.

content.heading: Go deeper: Devaluation and the two sides of the exchange rate
paragraphs: Devaluation lowers the price of domestic goods in foreign currency and raises the price of foreign goods at home. Nigerian exports of cocoa or sesame become cheaper to foreign buyers, so demand may expand, while imported fuel and machinery become dearer, so demand may contract. The payments balance improves only if those volume responses outweigh the higher import prices.

The exchange rate itself is set where demand meets supply of foreign currency. Foreign buyers demand naira to purchase Nigerian goods, investors demand naira to buy assets, and residents demand foreign currency to import or travel. Capital inflows raise demand for naira, while speculation can amplify a small movement into a sharp fall when traders expect further weakness.

Imported inflation tempers the gain. Much of Nigeria's fuel, food and equipment is priced abroad, so a weaker naira lifts domestic transport and production costs quickly. Export volumes adjust more slowly because contracts, shipping and buyer relationships take time to rearrange. That lag can worsen the balance briefly before it improves, which is the intuition behind the J-curve.

Revaluation is the mirror image: it makes imports cheaper and exports dearer, easing import prices but squeezing foreign sales. Depreciation under a floating rate achieves similar effects through market pressure rather than an official decision, while revaluation imposed by a central bank reflects a policy choice to strengthen the currency.
bullets: Devaluation cheapens exports and makes imports dearer.
The rate is set by demand for and supply of foreign currency.
Import pass-through can worsen the balance before depreciation helps.

lessons.title: International Economic Organisations
lessons.objective: Identify regional and global economic organisations, explain their functions, and assess their relevance and limits for Nigeria.

content.heading: International economic organisations
paragraphs: Nigeria borrows from the IMF, trades under WTO rules and belongs to ECOWAS, so international organisations shape its economy daily.

content.heading: Regional and continental organisations
paragraphs: A trader moves goods from Lagos to Cotonou without a visa while a Nigerian bank opens in Accra. Regional organisations make that movement easier.

ECOWAS promotes trade, free movement of persons, a common tariff and monetary cooperation among West African states; Nigeria hosts its headquarters in Abuja. The African Union promotes continental integration and peace, the EU is a customs union and single market, the ECA is the UN's regional economic commission for Africa, and the ADB finances African development projects.

Their relevance to Nigeria includes wider markets, cheaper imports, labour mobility, infrastructure finance and a stronger voice in world negotiations. Their limits are weak enforcement, overlapping memberships and uneven funding.
bullets: ECOWAS: West African trade and free movement.
AU and ECA: continental integration and research.
ADB: development finance.
content.takeaway: Regional bodies widen Nigeria's market and voice, but only when members enforce the rules.

check.question: The headquarters of ECOWAS is in ______.
check.why: The ECOWAS Commission is based in Abuja, Nigeria, which also hosts several of its institutions.

content.heading: Global financial and trade organisations
paragraphs: When Nigeria faces a balance-of-payments crisis, it may borrow from the IMF with conditions attached. Global institutions set the rules and supply the finance that national policy must work within.

The IMF lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems and advises on macro policy; the World Bank and its IBRD arm finance development projects; the WTO sets trade rules and settles disputes; UNCTAD studies trade and development; the OECD coordinates rich-country policy; the EEC was the forerunner of the EU.

Nigeria uses IMF stabilisation loans, World Bank and IBRD project finance, WTO trade rules and UNCTAD research. Loan conditions can require subsidy removal, privatisation and currency reform, which may be unpopular but restore external balance.
bullets: IMF: balance-of-payments loans.
World Bank and IBRD: development finance.
WTO: trade rules and disputes.
content.takeaway: Global institutions supply finance and rules, and both come with conditions.

check.question: The institution that lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems is the ______.
check.why: The IMF provides short- and medium-term balance-of-payments support, while the World Bank funds longer-term development projects.

visual.caption: The IMF stabilises a balance of payments; the World Bank finances development.

content.heading: OPEC and the relevance of these bodies to Nigeria
paragraphs: Nigeria's oil revenue rises and falls with OPEC decisions, so a quota meeting in Vienna can change the national budget.

OPEC coordinates the oil policies of member producers, sets production quotas and tries to stabilise prices; its major contribution to Nigeria is oil-price stabilisation. The relevance of international organisations to Nigeria includes export markets, development finance, technical advice, peacekeeping and a voice in trade negotiations.

Their limits include conditional loans, unequal bargaining power, quota restrictions on oil output and rules that open Nigerian markets to stronger foreign firms. Nigeria's response is to diversify exports, strengthen regional trade and negotiate rather than withdraw.
bullets: OPEC: quotas and oil-price stability.
Relevance: markets, finance, advice, voice.
Limits: conditions, quotas, unequal power.
content.takeaway: International organisations give Nigeria finance and markets, but they also constrain its choices.

check.question: The major contribution of OPEC to the Nigerian economy is the provision of ______.
check.why: OPEC coordinates production quotas to steady world oil prices, and stable prices steady Nigeria's oil revenue and budget.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: ECOWAS is regional; the IMF and World Bank are global. Do not mix their functions.

content.problem: Nigeria's OPEC quota is 1.5 million barrels per day and crude sells for $80 per barrel. Find the daily and annual oil revenue at full quota.

steps.reason: Multiply the quota by the price per barrel.
steps.predictPrompt: Now multiply by the days in a year.

steps.reason: Multiply daily revenue by 365 days.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: The quota caps output, so a lower quota or price cuts revenue even if costs are unchanged.
steps.result: At full quota and $80 oil, Nigeria earns about $43.8 billion a year; a quota cut or price fall reduces that directly.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Explain two benefits and one risk of Nigeria's membership of international economic organisations.
hints: Benefits include market access, development finance, technical advice and a stronger negotiating voice.
A risk is that loan conditions or trade rules limit national policy space.
A strong answer names a specific body and links it to a specific effect.

content.heading: Go deeper: How loan conditions steer a government's hands
paragraphs: Imagine Nigeria approves an IMF-supported programme. The money does not arrive as a free cheque. It is released in tranches, and each release depends on agreed checks, such as trimming fuel subsidies or tightening monetary control. The mechanism is that of an ordinary loan contract: the lender fears the cash will be spent without fixing what caused the crisis, so it ties the cash to behaviour.

Conditionality bundles two jobs. One is technical, because a country that overspends while borrowing abroad invites a debt spiral, and the lender wants assurance the gap will narrow. The other is disciplinary, because the conditions signal to other lenders that the government will stay on course. A missed review can therefore pause disbursement even when the damage is modest.

Compare the IMF with the World Bank. The Fund concentrates on short and medium term balance-of-payments strain, so its conditions touch exchange policy and fiscal discipline. The Bank, including its IBRD arm, more often funds named projects such as power or roads, so its conditions touch procurement and project management. The first asks whether the macro framework can hold; the second asks whether a project can be delivered without waste.

That distinction creates a dilemma. Conditions restoring external balance may raise transport fares or cut subsidies, and those costs fall first on urban workers and small traders. The exam point is not that conditions are good or bad, but that they transfer part of the policy choice from the elected government to the lender, and a top answer names who bears the adjustment.
bullets: Tranches link cash to policy compliance, not approval alone.
IMF conditions stress macro balance; World Bank conditions stress project delivery.
Adjustment costs fall unevenly, so ownership is part of the evaluation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why regional integration often stalls at the border
paragraphs: A free trade area removes tariffs among members, a customs union adds a common external tariff, a common market also frees movement of labour and capital, and a full economic union adds shared monetary policy. The ladder matters because each step removes another border cost. ECOWAS has climbed it unevenly, with formal commitments running ahead of daily enforcement.

Traders know the gap. A lorry may clear the formal tariff schedule yet still face roadblocks, divergent standards, informal levies and delays at ports. Firms price those delays into goods or stay within national markets where the rules are familiar. A common market needs predictable clearance, not merely a signed protocol.

Overlapping memberships sharpen the problem. Nigeria belongs to several regional groupings, and partners may follow different external tariffs or settle disputes differently. A preference granted in one bloc can be diluted by a rule in another, so businesses lobby for the rule that suits their route, while governments guard revenue linked to the old border.

For examinations, separate three layers. Name the formal stage, whether free trade or common market. Identify the non-tariff barrier that still bites. Judge effectiveness by trade flows, not treaty language. That order prevents the trap of calling every regional treaty a single market merely because tariffs have fallen.
bullets: Integration runs from tariff removal to factor mobility to shared policy.
Non-tariff barriers can undo formal tariff cuts.
Effectiveness is judged by flows and clearance time, not protocols.

content.heading: Go deeper: How a Vienna quota reaches the Nigerian budget
paragraphs: Start with the arithmetic a budget officer cannot escape. Revenue from crude equals price multiplied by volume actually lifted. OPEC acts mainly on volume through quotas, while world demand and refining capacity act heavily on price. A quota cut and a price slump therefore reinforce each other, while a quota rise during weak demand may lift volume without lifting revenue.

That arithmetic explains why Nigeria's budget feels procyclical. When oil money is plentiful, commitments on salaries, debt service and capital projects rise. When the quota or price falls, those commitments remain even though the cash has gone. The deficit that follows is the mismatch between sticky obligations and volatile petroleum receipts.

There is also an incentive problem inside any quota system. Each member would like others to cut while it sells more, because the price benefit is shared while extra volume accrues to one treasury. That free-rider pull is why discipline depends on monitoring and the willingness of large producers to restrain themselves. Suspicion of cheating alone can undo price support.

A strong answer links the quota to diversification without reciting a wishlist. Non-oil revenue matters because it follows a different cycle from crude, and regional trade matters because it uses demand oil cannot fully insure. Membership thus trades a voice in price stability for a ceiling on volume when revenue is most needed.
bullets: Oil revenue is price times quota volume, so both can fall together.
Sticky spending makes the budget procyclical under oil volatility.
Quota discipline is fragile because the gains from cheating are private.

lessons.title: Utility, Indifference Curves and Consumer Choice
lessons.objective: Distinguish total, average and marginal utility, use indifference curves and the budget line to find consumer equilibrium, and calculate consumer surplus.

content.heading: Consumer behaviour
paragraphs: Consumers choose among goods with limited income, and utility, indifference curves and consumer surplus explain those choices.

content.heading: Total, average and marginal utility
paragraphs: A student's first bottle of water after games is deeply satisfying; the fourth adds little.
Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good. It is subjective, and can be measured in utils (cardinal) or ranked (ordinal).

Total utility is the satisfaction from all units; average utility is total utility divided by units; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit. The law of diminishing marginal utility says marginal utility falls as consumption rises in a period. Total utility rises while marginal utility is positive, peaks where marginal utility is zero, and falls when marginal utility is negative.
Because marginal utility falls with quantity, a consumer buys more only at a lower price: the law of demand.
bullets: TU rises while MU > 0; peaks at MU = 0.
AU = TU ÷ Q; MU = change in TU ÷ change in Q.
Diminishing MU explains the downward-sloping demand curve.
content.takeaway: Each extra unit adds less satisfaction, which is why a lower price is needed to sell more.

check.question: Total utility is at its maximum when marginal utility is ______.
check.why: While marginal utility is positive, total utility is still rising; it stops rising at the point where the next unit adds nothing.

content.heading: Indifference curves, budget line and equilibrium
paragraphs: A shopper can afford several combinations of rice and beans, and some please her equally. The budget line shows what is affordable; the indifference curve shows equal satisfaction.
An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give equal satisfaction. It slopes downward, is convex because the marginal rate of substitution falls, and never crosses another.
A budget line shows the combinations a consumer can afford at given prices and income. Its slope is the price ratio; higher income shifts it outward, while a price change rotates it.

Consumer equilibrium occurs where the highest attainable indifference curve touches the budget line, so the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. A price fall raises real income and makes the good relatively cheaper; the income and substitution effects explain the higher quantity.
bullets: Indifference curve: equal satisfaction, convex.
Budget line: affordable combinations; slope = price ratio.
Equilibrium: MRS = price ratio.
content.takeaway: Equilibrium is where the budget line just touches the highest attainable indifference curve.

check.question: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give a consumer ______.
check.why: Every point on one indifference curve yields the same total utility, so the consumer is indifferent between them.

visual.caption: The cardinal approach measures utility; the ordinal approach ranks bundles.

rows.right: Indifference curves and the budget line

content.heading: Consumer surplus
paragraphs: A traveller would pay N2,000 for a bus fare but pays N1,200, so she gains N800. That gain is consumer surplus.
Consumer surplus is the difference between willingness to pay and the price actually paid. It measures the benefit of exchange.
On a demand curve, consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the market price, up to the quantity bought. A fall in price raises consumer surplus, and a rise in price reduces it.

The surplus explains the water-diamond paradox: water is vital but cheap because its marginal utility is low, while diamonds are frivolous but expensive because their marginal utility is high. Consumer surplus is used to judge the welfare effect of a price change, a tax or a subsidy.
bullets: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price paid.
Area below demand and above price.
A price fall raises surplus; a price rise cuts it.
content.takeaway: Consumer surplus measures the gain a buyer gets when the price is below what she would have paid.

check.question: Consumer surplus is the difference between the price a consumer is willing to pay and ______.
check.why: The surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the market price, not a cost or a utility total.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Utility is satisfaction, not usefulness. A useless ornament can give high utility, while a useful tool may give little.

content.problem: A consumer is willing to pay N500 for the first unit, N400 for the second and N300 for the third. The market price is N300. Find the consumer surplus.

steps.operation: Find the surplus on each unit
steps.reason: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the price actually paid.
steps.result: First unit: N500 − N300 = N200. Second: N400 − N300 = N100. Third: N300 − N300 = N0.
steps.predictPrompt: What is the total surplus?

steps.reason: Total consumer surplus is the sum of the gains on every unit bought.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: The consumer paid N900 for three units but was willing to pay N1,200.
steps.result: She gains N300, which is the area between her demand curve and the price.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: A consumer's income rises while prices stay constant. Explain the effect on the budget line and on the choice between two normal goods, distinguishing the income effect from the substitution effect.
hints: A rise in income shifts the budget line outward without changing its slope.
The income effect is the change in quantity caused by higher real income.
The substitution effect is the change caused by a good becoming cheaper relative to the other.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why each extra unit pleases less
paragraphs: The fall in marginal utility is not a law about molecules; it is a claim about attention and need. The first bottle of water after a match relieves thirst, the second adds comfort, and by the fourth the body signals that enough has been taken. Satisfaction declines because the sharpest want is already met, while each further unit competes for the same stomach and time.

Economists state the tendency with care. It assumes the consumer is roughly rational, the good is divisible into small units, and nothing else changes while units are added. Where that fails, the pattern can wobble. An addictive substance or a collectible that gains prestige with size can raise marginal utility for a while.

Cardinal and ordinal readings create a frequent exam trap. Cardinal utility assigns numbers such as utils to satisfaction, which lets a student add and average, but it pretends one person's 50 utils equals another's 50. Ordinal utility keeps only ranking, so it says one bundle is preferred without claiming the gap is twice as large. Modern theory therefore leans on indifference curves.

If each extra unit adds less, the buyer must sacrifice less to take it, so the market must offer the unit more cheaply. That is why diminishing marginal utility explains a downward-sloping demand curve through the shrinking value of the last unit, not merely restates it. The curve links lower price to larger quantity by that route.
bullets: Pleasure falls because the sharpest need is met first.
The law assumes divisibility and no change in other conditions.
Ordinal ranking avoids pretending satisfaction is countable across people.

content.heading: Go deeper: Corner cases where equilibrium refuses to sit in the middle
paragraphs: Picture a shopper who cares only about rice and not about beans. Her indifference curves are vertical, because extra beans add no satisfaction, and her optimum pushes all spending onto rice. The budget line still meets the highest attainable curve, but at a corner. The condition that the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio fails there, because shifting a naira from beans to rice would still gain even after the switch.

The opposite corner appears with goods consumed together, such as a phone and its charger. Satisfaction rises only when the pair grows, so the curves bend sharply toward the origin. The tangency rule predicts too much flexibility, because the shopper cannot trade one phone for three chargers. With perfect complements, price changes work mainly through the income effect.

Indivisibility creates another edge. A motorcycle or a school term cannot be bought in tiny slices, so the budget line is a guide rather than a continuous menu. The consumer may sit at the nearest whole point with money left over. When an exam asks why a textbook equilibrium is never reached, the answer is often that the good cannot be divided.

Price and income changes help separate the effects. A fall in one price rotates the budget line around the other intercept, while a rise in income shifts it outward in parallel. The rotation changes relative prices and therefore the substitution effect. The parallel shift changes only purchasing power and therefore the income effect. Naming which move is which is the quickest route to full marks.
bullets: Zero marginal value pushes the optimum to a corner.
Complements block substitution, so only income effects operate.
Lumpy goods make tangency approximate rather than exact.

content.heading: Go deeper: When consumer surplus misleads as a welfare ruler
paragraphs: Consumer surplus turns a price change into a welfare statement. A fall in price transfers money from sellers to buyers and lets buyers enjoy units once too dear. The drawn area grows twice: a rectangle on units already bought, plus a triangle on new units now worth buying. That double movement explains why a small price fall can feel like a large gain in transport or food markets.

Compare that ruler with producer surplus to see its limits. Producer surplus is the mirror gain sellers enjoy when price exceeds willingness to accept. A tax splits both gains, leaving the government with revenue and society with deadweight loss, while a subsidy merges them at the treasury's expense. The same diagram therefore grades taxes and subsidies as well as price moves.

Two cautions separate a top-band answer from a calculation. First, simple surplus treats every naira of gain and loss as equal, which hides that a naira matters more to a poor rider than to a wealthy passenger. Second, it assumes income effects are small, so willingness to pay is stable. Where a good absorbs a large budget share, such as housing, that strains.

Price controls sharpen the point. A ceiling inflates measured surplus on paper while creating queues that transfer the gain to those with time or connections. The calculation still describes willingness to pay, but distribution depends on how rationing is done. Good answers therefore append the method of allocation to any welfare claim.
bullets: Surplus captures both cheaper old units and newly worthwhile units.
Producer surplus is the seller mirror; taxes cut both sides.
Equal naira weighting hides who gains and rationing method.

lessons.title: National Income and Its Measurement
lessons.objective: Define GDP, GNP, NNP and national income, compare the output, income and expenditure approaches, and use the multiplier to find equilibrium income.

content.heading: National income and its measurement
paragraphs: National income measures the output of an economy, and its concepts decide what is counted and what is left out.

content.heading: Concepts and measurement
paragraphs: A country's factories, farms and offices produce goods and services all year; national income adds up their final value. The way that value is defined decides whether foreign-owned production or depreciation is included.

GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a year. GNP adds net factor income from abroad, NNP subtracts depreciation, and national income subtracts indirect taxes and adds subsidies to reach factor cost.

It can be measured by output (value added), income (rent, wages, interest, profit) or expenditure (C + I + G + X − M), and the three should agree. Only final goods count; intermediate goods, transfer payments and second-hand sales are excluded to avoid double counting. Nominal income uses current prices, real income uses constant prices, and per capita income divides national income by population.
bullets: GDP within borders; GNP by citizens; NNP after depreciation.
Output, income and expenditure should agree.
Real income uses constant prices; per capita divides by population.
content.takeaway: National income counts final output, not every payment that changes hands.

check.question: Gross domestic product measures the total value of goods and services produced ______.
options: by a country's citizens anywhere in the world
within a country in a year
check.why: GDP is a territorial measure: it counts production inside the country's borders, whoever owns the producer.

content.heading: Circular flow, consumption and saving
paragraphs: Workers spend part of their pay and save the rest, while firms borrow those savings to buy machines. Income circulates, but some leaks out and some is injected back.

In the circular flow, households supply land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship to firms, then spend their income on goods and services. The two-sector model has households and firms; the three-sector adds government, which taxes and spends.
Saving is income not consumed; investment is spending on capital goods. In the two-sector model, saving leaks and investment injects, so equilibrium needs S = I.

The consumption function is C = a + bY, where b is the marginal propensity to consume. APC and APS divide consumption and saving by income; MPC and MPS divide their changes by the change in income, and MPC + MPS = 1.
bullets: Households supply factors; firms supply goods.
Two-sector: S = I. Three-sector adds taxes and government spending.
APC + APS = 1 and MPC + MPS = 1.
content.takeaway: Income circulates between households and firms, and saving leaks while investment injects spending back.

check.question: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, the marginal propensity to save is ______.
check.why: Every extra naira of income is either consumed or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1 and MPS = 1 − 0.8.

visual.caption: The three-sector model adds government to the household-firm flow.

rows.right: Saving and taxes leak; investment and government spending inject

content.heading: Multiplier and equilibrium income
paragraphs: A new factory spends N100 million on machines, and the workers who build them spend part of their pay. One injection can raise income by more than its original size.
The multiplier is the number of times a change in spending multiplies into a larger change in income. It is k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), or 1 ÷ MPS.
Equilibrium income occurs where total spending equals output, or where injections equal leakages. In the two-sector model Y = C + I; in the three-sector model Y = C + I + G.

If MPC is 2/3, the multiplier is 3, so a N100 million rise in investment raises equilibrium income by N300 million. It is larger when people spend most of extra income, and smaller when they save or import a lot.
bullets: Change in income = k × change in investment.
Equilibrium: injections = leakages.
content.takeaway: A naira of new spending can create more than a naira of income when it is respent.

check.question: If the marginal propensity to consume is 2/3 and investment rises by N100 million, national income rises by ______.
check.why: The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 2/3) = 3, so N100 million × 3 = N300 million.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: GDP counts output within borders; GNP counts income earned by citizens. A foreign-owned factory in Nigeria counts in Nigeria's GDP, but its profit is not Nigerian GNP.

content.problem: An economy has a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75 and investment rises by N80 million. Find the multiplier and the change in equilibrium income.

steps.reason: The multiplier is one divided by one minus the marginal propensity to consume.
steps.predictPrompt: What does a multiplier of 4 mean?

steps.reason: Multiply the initial change in investment by the multiplier.
steps.result: Change in income = 4 × N80 million = N320 million.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: The extra income is larger than the initial injection because each round of spending becomes someone else's income.
steps.result: Income rises by N320 million, four times the N80 million injection.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: An economy's marginal propensity to consume is 0.75 and investment rises by N80 million. Calculate the multiplier and the change in income, and explain why the actual change may be smaller.
hints: Use k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC).
Multiply the injection by the multiplier.
Imports, spare capacity and crowding out can reduce the real effect.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why three ways of adding must agree
paragraphs: Output, income and expenditure are three windows onto the same hall of value. Every final good produced must be paid for by someone, and every payment must be received by some factor of production. With complete records the three totals coincide because they describe the same transactions from different sides.

The tightest test is the output method. It sums value added at each stage, meaning sales minus intermediate purchases from others. That subtraction stops wheat, flour and bread from being counted three times. The final product alone would give the same result if every stage were recorded, but value added is safer where stages are easy to miss.

Real economies bruise that equality in instructive places. A farmer who eats the yams she grows creates output without a market payment. An owner who lives in her own house supplies housing services without rent. Small traders with no books still produce value that may be understated. Statisticians assign reasoned estimates where no cash moves, and the honesty of the estimate is part of the method.

Transfer payments and second-hand sales mark the boundary. A pension or gift moves purchasing power without creating new output that year. A used car sold again moves ownership without new value, apart from any dealer's service. Counting them as fresh production is the classic double-counting error that inflates the total without enriching anyone.
bullets: Three methods agree because production, payment and receipt describe one flow.
Value added subtracts intermediates to avoid triple counting.
Imputed and informal output needs estimating where cash is absent.

content.heading: Go deeper: When the two-sector identity stretches to three and four
paragraphs: Start with the clean two-sector story. Households earn income, spend part and save the rest, while firms invest the amount saved. Equilibrium needs saving to equal investment, because any gap means stocks pile up or run down. If saving outruns investment, unsold goods accumulate, firms cut production and income falls until the gap closes.

Government widens the identity without changing its logic. Taxes leak income away from spending, while public spending injects demand back. Equilibrium becomes saving plus taxes equals investment plus government spending. A deficit, where spending exceeds taxes, is a net injection that supports income, and a surplus is a net leakage that dampens it.

The open economy adds imports as a leakage and exports as an injection. Saving plus taxes plus imports then equals investment plus government spending plus exports. Each term keeps its meaning from before, and balance is restored by income, exchange rates and policy, not by accounting trickery.

Examiners blur two identities that sound alike. The average shares must sum to one: average propensity to consume plus average propensity to save equals one. The marginal shares also sum to one, but they divide changes rather than levels. Stock versus flow is therefore the discrimination test.
bullets: Saving equals investment only after output adjusts to close the gap.
Government adds taxes as leakages and spending as injections.
Imports leak and exports inject, extending the same identity.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the multiplier shrinks as the economy opens
paragraphs: The multiplier works as an echo, not a single shout. An initial rise in investment becomes builders' income, who spend a share, whose spending becomes shopkeepers' income, and so on. Each round is smaller because part of every income leaks into saving, taxes or imports. The total is the sum of shrinking rounds, growing quickly when leakage is tiny and slowly when it is large.

That is why an open economy tames the multiplier. Where leakage is saving alone, the multiplier is the reciprocal of the marginal propensity to save. Let imports and taxes also absorb part of each extra naira, and the denominator grows. The same injection then finishes as a smaller multiple, because more of each round leaves the domestic loop.

Time adds a second taming mechanism. Rounds take time, prices may rise before output expands, and credit may tighten as demand grows. Where factories already run near full capacity, extra spending buys higher prices more than extra jobs. Where banks fear default, higher rates can crowd out the investment that started the chain. The textbook multiple becomes an upper bound.

A final trap is to multiply in the wrong direction. The multiplier scales an injection into an income change; it never turns an income change into an injection. If investment rises by 100 with a multiplier of three, income rises by 300. Confusing cause and echo reverses the story.
bullets: The multiplier sums shrinking rounds of respent income.
Imports and taxes add leakages, so the multiple falls.
Capacity, prices and credit can truncate the textbook echo.

lessons.title: Economic Growth and Development
lessons.objective: Distinguish growth from development, identify development indicators and Nigerian obstacles, and explain the role and limits of development planning.
