content.heading: Economic growth and development
paragraphs: Growth is a bigger economy; development is a better one, and the difference matters when a country's output rises while poverty persists.

content.heading: Growth versus development
paragraphs: A country's oil output doubles, but schools, hospitals and incomes outside oil barely change. Output grew; development did not.

Economic growth is a sustained rise in real national output, usually measured by real GDP or GDP per capita. Economic development is broader: it adds health, education, income distribution, infrastructure and structural change.

Growth can occur without development if the extra output is concentrated in one sector or region, or if population grows as fast as output. Development requires both rising output and better living conditions. Indicators include GDP per capita, life expectancy, literacy, school enrolment, access to clean water, the Human Development Index and the poverty rate; no single indicator captures development, so they are read together.
bullets: Growth: more output. Development: more output plus better lives.
Oil output can grow while schools and incomes stagnate.
HDI combines income, health and education.
content.takeaway: Growth measures the size of the economy; development measures the quality of life it supports.

check.question: A major feature of an underdeveloped economy is ______.
options: a low level of standard of living
a low rate of population growth
check.why: Underdevelopment shows in low incomes, poor health and education and weak infrastructure, not in high capacity use or low unemployment.

content.heading: Factors and Nigerian problems
paragraphs: A country with fertile land and oil still imports food and refined fuel, because its refineries, roads and skills are weak. Resources alone do not produce development.

Growth and development depend on natural resources, human capital, capital formation, technology, infrastructure, institutions and political stability. Savings and investment fund capital, while education and health raise productivity.

Nigeria's problems include over-dependence on oil, weak infrastructure, corruption and poor governance, insecurity, low human-capital development, a narrow export base and dependence on imported manufactures. A large population can be a market and a workforce, but it becomes a burden when jobs and skills do not grow with it.
bullets: Resources, human capital, capital, technology, infrastructure, institutions.
Nigeria: oil dependence, weak infrastructure, corruption, insecurity.
Population is an asset only when skills and jobs grow.
content.takeaway: Resources do not develop an economy; the institutions and skills that use them do.

check.question: Which is a problem of development in Nigeria?
check.why: Oil supplies most export earnings and government revenue, so a fall in oil prices or output destabilises the whole budget and economy.

visual.caption: Growth is a quantity; development is a set of improvements.

rows.right: Rising output plus better living conditions

rows.left: Real GDP and GDP per capita

content.heading: Development planning in Nigeria
paragraphs: Nigeria has launched successive national plans, yet many targets were missed because funding, data and political will fell short.
Development planning sets targets for output, employment, infrastructure and social services, and allocates resources to meet them. It can coordinate investment and focus government effort.

Nigeria used fixed national development plans after independence, then rolling plans, the Vision 20:2020 strategy, the Economic Recovery and Growth Plan and the National Development Plan. The plans usually aimed at diversification, infrastructure and human capital. They often failed because of unstable funding, poor data, corruption, policy inconsistency and weak implementation; a plan without a budget, monitoring and accountability remains a document rather than a strategy.
bullets: Planning sets targets and allocates resources.
Nigeria: fixed plans, rolling plans, Vision 20:2020, ERGP, NDP.
Failure: funding, data, corruption, inconsistency, weak implementation.
content.takeaway: A development plan works only when the budget, data and accountability behind it work.

check.question: A major reason Nigerian development plans underperform is ______.
check.why: Plans are often well written but poorly funded, monitored and implemented, so targets are missed.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Growth and development are not synonyms. GDP can rise while poverty, literacy and health stay unchanged.

content.problem: Real GDP grows from N80 trillion to N88 trillion while population grows from 200 million to 220 million. Find the growth in total output and in output per person, and say whether living standards rose.

steps.reason: Divide the change in real GDP by the original GDP.
steps.predictPrompt: Now find GDP per person before and after.

steps.reason: Divide real GDP by population in each year.
steps.result: Before: N80 trillion ÷ 200 million = N400,000. After: N88 trillion ÷ 220 million = N400,000.
steps.predictPrompt: In your own words, why does this step come before the next one?

steps.reason: Total output rose, but population rose by the same proportion.
steps.result: Output per person is unchanged, so average living standards did not rise.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: Nigeria's GDP has grown, but poverty remains widespread. Explain two reasons why growth may not translate into development, and one policy that would connect them.
hints: Growth may be concentrated in oil or in cities, leaving other sectors and regions behind.
Population growth can absorb the extra output, leaving income per head flat.
Link the policy to jobs, skills or social spending, not just to more output.

content.heading: Go deeper: How output can rise while lives barely change
paragraphs: Imagine a mine or oil field on the edge of an otherwise stagnant economy. Production in that enclave can double while cassava farmers, market traders and clinic attendants see no gain. GDP rises, yet jobs barely move, because the booming activity uses few local workers and buys few local inputs. Growth that fails to spread is growth in a fence.

That pattern has a name in textbooks: enclave growth. Its mechanism is sectoral concentration. One sector dominates export earnings and government revenue, while the rest stagnates for lack of credit, power and skills. When the dominant price falls, the whole budget wobbles even though other sectors never benefited strongly.

Population can erase the same gain more quietly. Suppose real output grows by ten per cent while population grows by ten per cent as well. Output per head stays flat, classrooms fill further, and clinic queues lengthen. The aggregate figure celebrates expansion the average family cannot feel, which is why per capita correction is the heart of welfare judgement.

Indicators beyond GDP try to catch what the fence hides. Life expectancy and literacy capture health and knowledge, clean water captures daily dignity, and poverty rates capture how many people growth reached. No single number carries the whole story, so wise readers compare the family of measures rather than crowning one index.
bullets: Enclave growth concentrates gains in one sector or city.
Per capita figures decide whether expansion reaches the average family.
Health, schooling and poverty reveal what GDP totals hide.

content.heading: Go deeper: The vicious circle and how it is broken
paragraphs: The classic vicious circle of poverty runs on a loop. Low income leaves little saving, little saving funds little investment, little investment keeps productivity low, and low productivity holds income down. Each link feeds the next, so a market for manufactures never grows large enough to justify modern factories. The circle describes a trap, not a single defect.

Two older strategies attacked the loop from opposite sides. Balanced growth spreads investment across many sectors so agriculture and industry buy from each other. The big push concentrates investment in a coordinated burst, such as power, ports and factories together, so no single project fails for want of the others. Both accept that scattered spending may be too timid.

Modern accounts add human capital and institutions to the loop. A worker with basic literacy and reliable health uses machines more productively, and a contract courts will enforce invites saving to become investment. Those factors raise the return on physical capital. A road still helps, but a road plus skilled drivers and maintenance funding helps more.

Population shows why context decides the verdict. A young age structure can supply workers and customers when schools and jobs expand with it. The same structure becomes a burden when classrooms lack teachers and cities lack formal jobs. The dividend is conditional: skills and employment must grow ahead of numbers.
bullets: Low income, saving, investment and productivity trap each other in a circle.
Balanced growth spreads bets; a big push coordinates them.
Skills and enforceable rules raise the payoff from every project.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why a plan on paper is not a plan in practice
paragraphs: A national plan sets multi-year targets for power, roads, jobs and schooling. The annual budget, however, decides what is actually funded next year. The gap between the two documents is where many Nigerian plans weaken. A target in the plan but not in the budget line is a wish, and a budget line without monitoring is a hope rather than a strategy.

Fixed plans assume the future can be fixed in advance, while rolling plans revise targets as fresh data arrives. Rolling discipline suits economies battered by oil swings, but it demands honest statistics and regular review. Without both, rolling becomes drifting: each year borrows the language of the next without confronting the bottleneck identified last year.

Federal structure adds a second gap. The national government may plan a corridor crossing several states, yet states control land, local implementation and much staffing. Coordination failures and mismatched priorities can strand a project between tiers. A plan that ignores who builds, who maintains and who pays to run the asset is unfinished on arrival.

Evaluation closes the loop or exposes its absence. A plan earns the name strategy only when outcomes are measured, officials answer for variance, and the next budget follows the evidence. Examiners therefore link failed implementation to unstable funding, poor data, corruption and inconsistency as a bundle. Together they explain a pattern, not a single miss.
bullets: The annual budget, not the plan document, is where targets live or die.
Rolling plans need data and review, or revision becomes drift.
Federal coordination and evaluation decide whether targets become assets.

lessons.title: Financial Institutions and Markets
lessons.objective: Identify the types of financial institutions, distinguish the money and capital markets, explain credit creation, and describe monetary policy and financial regulation in Nigeria.

content.heading: Financial institutions
paragraphs: A trader saves part of her profit while a transport firm needs a loan, and the financial system links the two.

content.heading: Types of financial institutions
paragraphs: A trader saves with a commercial bank, which lends part of the money to a transport firm. Several institutions move funds from savers to borrowers.

Deposit money banks accept deposits and lend, mostly short term. Merchant banks handle wholesale and corporate finance; development banks supply long-term project finance; mortgage banks and building societies finance housing; microfinance banks serve small borrowers; insurance companies and pension funds invest long-term funds. Traditional lenders such as moneylenders and cooperative societies also lend, often outside formal regulation.
The Central Bank of Nigeria is the apex institution. It issues currency, acts as banker to government and banks, lends as lender of last resort and supervises the system.
bullets: Banks take deposits and create credit.
Development banks fund long-term projects.
The CBN regulates; it does not compete for customers.
content.takeaway: Financial institutions channel savings into investment, and the CBN supervises the channel.

check.question: Development banks in Nigeria are mainly established to provide ______.
check.why: Development banks supply patient finance for agriculture, industry and infrastructure, which commercial banks rarely fund on a long horizon.

content.heading: Money and capital markets, and money creation
paragraphs: A bank holds only a fraction of deposits as cash, because most depositors do not withdraw at once. It lends the rest, and each loan returns as a new deposit elsewhere.

That is credit creation: with a cash reserve ratio of 20 per cent, a N1,000 deposit supports N5,000 of deposits, since the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.2. Leakages into cash, excess reserves and imports shrink the real expansion.

The money market handles short-term funds: treasury bills, commercial paper and interbank loans. The capital market handles long-term funds: shares and bonds traded on the Nigerian Exchange, with the Securities and Exchange Commission as regulator. Firms use the money market for working capital and the capital market for expansion.
bullets: Money market: short term, under a year.
Capital market: shares and bonds, long term.
Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio.
content.takeaway: Banks create deposits by lending, but the money and capital markets serve different time horizons.

check.question: Short-term loans for investment are usually obtained through the ______.
check.why: The money market trades instruments that mature within a year, so it suits short-term working capital rather than long-term expansion.

visual.caption: The money market is short term; the capital market is long term.

content.heading: Regulation, monetary policy and Nigerian challenges
paragraphs: When inflation rises, the CBN can make credit dearer or scarcer. Its instruments work through the cost and supply of bank reserves. Open market operations sell bills to mop up reserves, while a higher cash reserve ratio cuts the funds banks can lend.

Regulators include the CBN for banks, the NDIC for deposit insurance, the SEC for the capital market, NAICOM for insurance and PenCom for pensions. Monetary policy uses open market operations, the cash reserve ratio, the monetary policy rate, special deposits, moral suasion and direct controls.

Nigeria's financial institutions face high non-performing loans, thin capital, fraud, financial exclusion, exchange-rate pressure and weak consumer protection. Raising capital, enforcing credit rules and expanding mobile and agent banking are the standard responses.
bullets: Regulators: CBN, NDIC, SEC, NAICOM, PenCom.
Instruments: OMO, CRR, MPR, special deposits.
Challenges: bad loans, fraud, exclusion.
content.takeaway: Regulation and monetary policy decide how safely banks can turn deposits into credit.

check.question: Foreign exchange control in Nigeria is administered by the ______.
check.why: The CBN manages the external reserves and the exchange rate, so it administers foreign exchange control rather than the banks or the SEC.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: The CBN is banker to the government and to the banks. A commercial bank is banker to the public.

content.problem: A bank receives a new deposit of N50,000 and the cash reserve ratio is 20 per cent. Find the credit multiplier and the total deposits the banking system can create.

steps.reason: The credit multiplier is one divided by the cash reserve ratio.
steps.predictPrompt: What does a multiplier of 5 mean?

steps.reason: Multiply the new deposit by the multiplier to get total deposits.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: The bank keeps 20 per cent as reserves and lends the rest, and each loan returns as a deposit.
steps.result: The N50,000 deposit supports N250,000 of deposits, with N200,000 created as credit.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.question: A manufacturing firm needs N200 million for a new plant that will take five years to build. Explain whether it should raise the money in the money market or the capital market, and name one regulator it will deal with.
hints: Match the maturity of the instrument to the life of the project.
The money market is for short-term funds; the capital market is for long-term funds.
The SEC regulates the capital market, while the CBN regulates the banks.

content.heading: Go deeper: How one deposit becomes many without printing money
paragraphs: Follow a cheque for N100,000 moving through the system. The receiving bank sets aside the required fraction as reserves, often illustrated at twenty per cent. It can lend the remaining N80,000, which the borrower may spend with a customer of another bank. That bank again sets aside reserves and lends the balance. Each handoff is smaller, yet deposits sum across banks.

The tidy ladder rests on habits real banks only approximate. Customers must redeposit quickly rather than hoard cash, banks must lend rather than sit on excess reserves, and borrowers must be deemed creditworthy. Cash withdrawals leak, idle reserves thin the ladder, and imports send spending abroad where the chain cannot continue. The textbook multiple is an idealised ceiling, not a forecast.

A second confusion matters for examinations. The reserve ratio limits how much deposit money the system can support on a given base of reserves, while the base is cash and reserves at the central bank. Printing more base money is the central bank's act. Lending more against the same base is the commercial banks' act. Both expand broad money, but through different doors.

Capital and confidence bind the ladder from the other side. A bank must hold enough own funds to absorb losses and keep depositors believing their balances are safe. When default fears rise, banks lend less willingly and customers withdraw faster. Credit contracts though the rule has not changed, which shows rules set the outer limit while trust sets the pace.
bullets: Loans return as deposits elsewhere, so the system expands beyond one bank.
Cash hoarding, excess reserves and imports shrink the ladder.
Reserves limit the ceiling; capital and trust decide the climb.

content.heading: Go deeper: Matching the instrument to the life of the project
paragraphs: The first question in any fundraising choice is time. A trader who needs stock for the festive season will sell within months, so funding must repay within months. A manufacturer who needs a factory earning for years cannot repay from a three-month loan without frantic refinancing. Maturity matching is prudence, not pedantry.

The money market serves the short end. Treasury bills, commercial paper and interbank placements mature inside a year, so they suit working capital, seasonal inventories and trade credit. The capital market serves the long end. Shares carry no fixed maturity and claim a share of earnings, while bonds promise payments over several years. Firms use the first market to keep moving and the second to keep growing.

The primary and secondary markets add a second distinction. In the primary market a company sells new securities and receives the proceeds. In the secondary market, such as the Nigerian Exchange, investors trade securities already issued, and no new cash reaches the company. A rising price enriches holders but funds the firm only when it issues anew.

For exams, make the choice step by step. Name the payback period, rule out any instrument maturing far sooner or later, then name the regulator for what remains. A five-year plant points to bonds or shares under capital-market oversight, not to a treasury bill. That chain earns more than reciting market names.
bullets: Short needs belong in the money market; long needs in the capital market.
Primary issues fund the firm; secondary trading only transfers ownership.
Regulator follows the market: central bank versus securities oversight.

content.heading: Go deeper: Runs, guarantees and the lender behind the counter
paragraphs: A bank run begins with doubt rather than insolvency. If depositors fear others will withdraw first, each has reason to withdraw early even if the bank is sound. Because banks lend much of their deposits for longer terms, they cannot repay everyone at once. Doubt becomes withdrawal, withdrawal becomes forced borrowing, and forced borrowing can turn doubt into failure.

Deposit insurance breaks that logic by guaranteeing small balances, as the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation does within its statutory limits. A depositor who trusts the guarantee need not race the queue. That promise calms panic, but it also softens discipline, because a bank may attract deposits with high rates while taking larger risks. Insurance thus trades one fragility for another.

The lender of last resort stands behind the insurance as the final buffer. The Central Bank of Nigeria can lend to a solvent yet illiquid bank whose assets exceed liabilities but whose cash is tied up in loans. Help is necessary in a crisis, yet helping too easily teaches bankers rescue is assured. Collateral and supervisory pressure try to keep the buffer from becoming a cushion.

Cosmetic fixes rarely address the root. Higher capital forces owners to share losses before depositors do, prompt corrective action restructures ailing banks earlier, and credible audits reveal weak assets sooner. Mobile and agent banking expand inclusion without changing this logic. Keep the roles distinct: insurance protects depositors, the lender protects liquidity, capital protects discipline.
bullets: Runs feed on fear because deposits are lent for longer terms.
Insurance calms depositors but softens their discipline.
The lender steadies liquidity without excusing weak solvency.

lessons.title: Public Finance, Taxation and the Budget
lessons.objective: Explain the objectives and revenue sources of public finance, classify taxes and their incidence, and describe fiscal policy, budgets, public debt and revenue allocation in Nigeria.

content.heading: Public finance
paragraphs: A state government builds a road with money raised from companies and from the oil federation account. Public finance studies how it raises and spends that money.

content.heading: Objectives, revenue and expenditure
paragraphs: Public finance aims at providing public goods, redistributing income, stabilising the economy, protecting infant industries and promoting growth. Public goods such as defence and street lighting are non-excludable and non-rival, so markets underprovide them.

Revenue comes from taxes, royalties, rents, fees, licences, fines, dividends from state enterprises, grants and aid. Royalties and rents come mainly from oil and mining, while fees, licences and fines come from regulation. Borrowing is not true revenue; it creates a future obligation.

Public expenditure is recurrent (salaries, allowances, debt service, running costs) or capital (roads, schools, hospitals, power). Capital spending adds to productive capacity, while recurrent spending maintains it. Heavy borrowing for either can crowd out private investment.
bullets: Revenue: taxes, royalties, rents, fees, grants, aid.
Recurrent: salaries and running costs.
Capital: roads, schools, hospitals.
content.takeaway: Public finance is about what government takes, what it spends and why.

check.question: All of the following are sources of government revenue except ______.
options: personal income, disposable income and transfer earnings
check.why: Personal income and transfer earnings belong to households; government revenue comes from taxes, fees, dividends, grants, aid and borrowing.

content.heading: Principles, types and incidence of taxation
paragraphs: A market woman pays VAT on a bag of rice without filling any form, while a salaried worker's income tax is deducted at source. The taxes differ in how they are collected and who bears them.

Tax principles include equity, certainty, convenience, economy and flexibility. Direct taxes fall on income and wealth, such as personal income tax and company tax; indirect taxes fall on goods and services, such as VAT, import duty and excise duty.

A progressive tax takes a larger share from higher incomes, a proportional tax takes the same rate, and a regressive tax takes a larger share from lower incomes. Incidence is who finally bears the burden: a tax on sellers can shift forward to consumers through higher prices or backward to suppliers. Taxes can discourage work and investment and encourage evasion.
bullets: Direct: income and wealth. Indirect: goods and services.
Progressive, proportional, regressive.
Incidence: who finally pays.
content.takeaway: The person who hands over a tax is not always the person who bears it.

check.question: Value added tax is an example of ______.
check.why: VAT is charged on the sale of goods and services and passed through prices, so it is an indirect tax whatever the seller's income.

visual.caption: Direct tax is assessed on the person; indirect tax is charged on the transaction.

content.heading: Fiscal policy, budgets, debt and revenue allocation
paragraphs: When a recession cuts revenue, government can spend more or tax less to revive demand. Fiscal policy is the use of taxation and spending to influence the economy.

Its instruments are taxation, government expenditure, subsidies, grants and public borrowing. A budget surplus means revenue exceeds expenditure, a deficit means expenditure exceeds revenue, and a balanced budget means they are equal. Deficits are financed by borrowing, which creates public debt; domestic borrowing can crowd out private investment, while external borrowing brings exchange-rate risk.

Nigeria shares revenue through the federation account using derivation, population, equality and land mass, with shares for states and local governments. Resource control is the claim of producing areas to a larger share of the resources taken from them, and the Niger Delta dispute is the clearest example.
bullets: Fiscal policy: taxes and spending.
Surplus, deficit, balanced budget.
Allocation: derivation, population, equality, land mass.
content.takeaway: A budget is a plan, and a deficit is a debt postponed, not avoided.

check.question: A budget deficit occurs when ______.
check.why: A deficit is the gap left when planned spending is greater than expected revenue, and it must be financed by borrowing.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: VAT is indirect even though the seller hands it over. The tax is on the sale, and the seller passes it to government.

content.problem: A trader buys a good for N4,000 and sells it for N5,000, and VAT is 7.5 per cent. Find the VAT the trader remits and the price the consumer pays.

steps.reason: VAT is charged on the selling price, not on the trader's profit.
steps.predictPrompt: What is 7.5 per cent of N5,000?

steps.reason: Multiply the selling price by the VAT rate.
steps.predictPrompt: Which numbers or terms work with each other first?

steps.reason: The consumer pays the price plus the tax, and the trader remits the tax.
steps.result: Consumer pays N5,375, and the trader remits N375 to government.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Government wants to reduce a budget deficit without cutting capital projects. Name two options and one risk of each.
hints: It can raise tax revenue or cut recurrent spending.
It can also borrow, but that adds debt-service costs and may crowd out private investment.
A strong answer notes the trade-off between short-term relief and long-term growth.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why borrowing is not revenue and how debt compounds
paragraphs: Revenue is income government can command without creating an offsetting obligation. Tax, royalties, rents, fees and grants fit. Borrowing does not, because the cash arrives alongside a promise to repay with interest. Treating borrowed cash as revenue flatters the budget while hiding the future claim on later taxpayers.

The deficit and the debt are easily confused. The deficit is the gap in one year when spending exceeds revenue. The debt is the accumulated stock of past gaps still unpaid. A government can cut a deficit yet still carry heavy debt service, just as a household can stop adding to a loan yet still owe instalments. The flow is the problem of the year; the stock is the burden that remains.

Domestic and external borrowing burden the economy by different routes. Debt sold at home competes for loanable funds, so when government borrows heavily, private firms face dearer credit and investment is crowded out. Debt owed abroad must be serviced from export earnings, so depreciation of the naira raises the local cost of the same dollar obligation even when no new loan is taken.

Sustainability is therefore a qualitative judgement, not a magic number. Debt is manageable when growth and revenue together outrun the interest burden, and precarious when interest consumes the budget faster than services improve. Borrowing to build power or ports that raise future output differs from borrowing to pay salaries, because the second leaves no asset to service its liability.
bullets: Borrowing adds cash and an obligation, so it is financing, not revenue.
The deficit is a yearly flow; the debt is the lasting stock.
Domestic debt crowds out firms; foreign debt exposes the budget to depreciation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Who truly bears a tax and why the seller is beside the point
paragraphs: Statutory incidence is who hands money to government; economic incidence is who finally bears the burden. A trader remits value added tax and a company remits corporation tax, yet both can pass part of the pain onward. The trader raises price; the company accepts lower profit or pays suppliers less. The cheque tells one story; the shifting tells another.

The shifting follows relative flexibility. When buyers can easily postpone or switch, demand is elastic and sellers absorb more, because raising price would lose sales. When buyers have no alternative, demand is inelastic and consumers absorb more through higher prices. The less elastic side carries the larger share, whether the tax falls on buyers or sellers.

That logic explains why the same tax can feel unfair depending on the base. A proportional income tax takes the same rate from all, yet low earners spend every naira while high earners save part, so the felt burden can be heavier at the bottom. A progressive schedule raises the rate with income, while a flat excise on a necessity strikes poorer households hardest in proportion to means.

Good design weighs efficiency against fairness and collection costs. A broad tax with few exemptions is harder to evade than a narrow tax full of loopholes, while a tax discouraging work narrows the base it seeks to command. The exam skill is to name the direction of shifting first, then the factor deciding its size.
bullets: The remitter is not necessarily the bearer of the burden.
The less elastic side of the market carries more of the tax.
Progressivity is judged on the burden relative to means, not the rate alone.

content.heading: Go deeper: How derivation and equalisation argue inside one federation account
paragraphs: Every federation account must answer two questions at once. Should the area producing oil or minerals keep more of what it generates? Should poorer areas be lifted toward a common standard even if they generate less? Derivation favours the first, equalisation the second, and Nigeria's formula blends both with population, equality of states and land mass.

Derivation in practice means the producing state receives a share of revenue from resources within its borders before the remainder is pooled. Its virtue is that it rewards production and may calm resource-control agitation. Its cost is that oil and mineral states pull ahead while others fall behind, stretching the gap federalism is meant to narrow.

Population and equality pull the other way. Population shares follow need for schools, clinics and roads, while an equality weight gives every state a base amount. Land mass favours vast, sparsely settled states whose costs spread across distance. Together these tilt the pool toward equalisation, which protects citizenship across the federation but can dull the incentive to raise internal revenue.

A strong answer states the trade-off rather than crowning one criterion. Derive strongly and production is rewarded while cohesion frays. Equalise strongly and cohesion holds while collection effort weakens. The Niger Delta debate illumines the same tension, because a larger derivation share is at once a claim about justice, compensation and control.
bullets: Derivation rewards producing areas; equalisation lifts poorer areas.
Population follows service need; equality guarantees a base share.
The formula trades incentive against cohesion, so no single criterion rules.

lessons.title: Agriculture in Nigeria
lessons.objective: Describe the types and features of Nigerian agriculture, explain its role in development, and assess its problems, policies and income instability.

content.heading: Agriculture in Nigeria
paragraphs: A farmer in Benue plants yam on a small plot while a plantation in Cross River employs hundreds. Both show how agriculture is organised in Nigeria.

content.heading: Types and features of agriculture
paragraphs: A family farms a small plot with hoes and sells only the surplus, while a plantation employs wage labour and grows one crop for sale. These are the two ends of Nigerian agriculture.

Subsistence farming produces mainly for the family, while commercial farming produces for sale. Peasant or smallholder farming dominates, alongside plantation and large-scale mechanised farms. Most farms are rain-fed, labour-intensive and small, with low use of fertiliser and machinery.

Farming is seasonal, depends on land tenure and weather, and yields are low because inputs, credit and extension services are weak. Large-scale farming can conduct research and employ labour on a large scale, but it needs capital and management that most smallholders lack.
bullets: Subsistence for the family; commercial for sale.
Smallholdings dominate; rain-fed and labour-intensive.
Large scale: research, machinery, wage labour.
content.takeaway: Nigerian agriculture is mostly small, rain-fed and seasonal, and that shape explains its low yields.

check.question: An advantage of large-scale farming over peasant farming is ______.
options: encouraging the use of traditional implements
conducting research and employing labour on a large scale
check.why: Large farms can fund research, machinery and wage labour, while peasant farms rely on family labour and simple tools.

visual.caption: Subsistence feeds the family; commercial farming sells the output.

content.heading: The role of agriculture in development
paragraphs: Agriculture feeds the country, employs most of the rural population and supplies factories with cotton, cocoa and groundnuts. Its health decides whether the rest of the economy can grow.

It provides food and guarantees food security, employs a large share of the population, supplies raw materials to industry, earns foreign exchange through cash crops and provides a market for industrial goods. It also supplies savings and tax revenue for development. Its share of GDP has fallen as oil grew, but its share of employment remains high.

Agriculture contributes to development by releasing labour to industry, feeding growing towns and raising rural incomes. When it stagnates, food prices rise, imports grow and industry loses its raw materials.
bullets: Food, jobs, raw materials, exports, markets.
Releases labour to industry.
Stagnation raises food prices and imports.
content.takeaway: Agriculture is the base that feeds and supplies the rest of the economy.

check.question: The most important function of agriculture to the Nigerian economy is ______.
check.why: Food is the first requirement of any economy, so feeding the population is agriculture's most important function.

content.heading: Problems, policies and income instability
paragraphs: A tomato farmer watches a good harvest rot because the road is bad and no cold store exists. Good weather can lower his income rather than raise it.

Problems include low mechanisation, insecure land tenure, weak credit, poor storage and transport, pests, climate risk and an ageing workforce. Policies include the Green Revolution, Operation Feed the Nation, the Anchor Borrowers' Programme, fertiliser subsidies, extension services and credit guarantees, though poor funding and implementation have limited their effect.

Farm incomes are unstable because supply depends on weather, prices swing between harvest and lean seasons, and produce is perishable. Irrigation, storage, commodity boards, price stabilisation, cooperatives, insurance and access to markets reduce the instability.
bullets: Problems: inputs, land, credit, storage, climate.
Policies: subsidies, credit, extension, Anchor Borrowers.
Instability: weather, prices, perishability.
content.takeaway: Farming fails less from lazy farmers than from weak inputs, storage and markets.

check.question: An important role of agriculture in an economy is ______.
check.why: Agriculture employs a large share of the population, especially in rural areas, and that employment is a major economic role.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Agriculture includes crop farming, livestock, forestry and fishing, so all four count in agricultural output.

content.problem: A farmer harvests 2,000 kg of tomatoes. He sells 1,500 kg at N400 per kg and loses 500 kg to spoilage. Find his revenue and the value lost.

steps.reason: Revenue is the quantity sold multiplied by the price.
steps.predictPrompt: What would the spoiled tomatoes have been worth?

steps.reason: The spoiled quantity is valued at the same market price.
steps.predictPrompt: In your own words, why does this step come before the next one?

steps.reason: Storage or a better road would have turned the loss into sales.
steps.result: Better storage would have raised his income by N200,000, a third of his potential revenue.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: A state wants to raise farm incomes and reduce rural poverty. Explain two policies it could use and one risk of each.
hints: Think about inputs, credit, storage, roads, extension or price support.
A subsidy can raise output but strain the budget and encourage smuggling.
Storage and roads cut post-harvest losses, but they need maintenance.

content.heading: Go deeper: How land tenure shapes what a farmer plants
paragraphs: Land tenure is the rule that decides who may use a parcel, for how long, and what may be taken from it. Where use rests on family or communal allocation, a farmer may grow yam for one season yet hesitate to plant cocoa or build irrigation. The hesitation is rational: effort spent on a tree that matures after the user loses the plot benefits the next occupant.

Formal title changes the calculation only when it is secure, transferable and cheap to enforce. A certificate of occupancy can let a farmer rent, pledge or sell land, raise credit and plan beyond one harvest. Where paperwork is slow or contested, title adds cost without adding confidence, and many households prefer customary security neighbours recognise.

Access is uneven by gender and status within the customary system. Women may farm through husbands or fathers rather than hold land themselves, while young men wait for inheritance. Rental and borrowing fill the gap, but a borrower will not fund drainage or soil building on a plot that can be reclaimed after one season.

Separate tenure from farm size when answering questions. A small holding with secure inheritance can sustain intensive care, while a larger borrowed plot remains starved of fertiliser and pruning. Tenure is best read as an incentive: the weaker the right to stay, the shorter the horizon of investment.
bullets: Weak tenure shortens the investment horizon.
Secure transferable rights support long-term soil and tree investment.
Borrowed plots rarely justify permanent improvements.

content.heading: Go deeper: Cash and food crops pull in opposite directions
paragraphs: A household must choose between feeding itself and selling for cash. Food crops such as yam, cassava, maize and rice are grown largely for consumption, harvested when the family needs them and stored informally. Cash crops such as cocoa, cotton, rubber or groundnuts are graded, transported to processors or ports, and paid at a price set far from the farm.

Marketing pulls the two apart. Food crops face local demand that spikes in the lean season, rewarding those who can store and sell later. Cash crops face export and factory demand, where quality, timing and volume decide the price, so a cash-crop grower may earn coins yet buy dearer food.

Geography sharpens the split. Cereals dominate the drier north, tubers and roots the middle belt, and tree crops the wetter south, though each zone now trades across those borders. Cash-crop zones earn foreign exchange through exports, yet reliance on one export exposes them to world price falls.

The examination discrimination is about purpose. Ask whether output is consumed, sold locally or exported, and the answer tells you which price matters. Higher export earnings have not fed anyone and lower food prices have not enriched an export farmer, so strength lies in raising surplus from both so food is secure and cash can finance the next season.
bullets: Food crops feed the household; cash crops earn market income.
Different buyers set different prices for the two purposes.
Export success is not the same as food security.

content.heading: Go deeper: Post-harvest loss and the cobweb of farm prices
paragraphs: Loss after harvest follows a chain. A ripe tomato softens within days, a washed-out road delays the lorry, and a market without cold storage accepts whatever the trader brings. Each break cuts quantity sold and quality fetched, so the farmer harvests into a glut and sells at the lowest price of the year.

Farm prices swing further because planting replies to last season's price. High prices invite heavy planting, the next harvest floods the market, prices fall, farmers withdraw, supply tightens and prices rise again. This cobweb repeats most violently for annual crops, where the reply is immediate at the next sowing.

Storage, processing and contracts break the cycle. A warehouse receipt lets a farmer hold grain instead of dumping it, a processor who buys forward fixes a price before harvest, and a cooperative that bulks produce can negotiate transport. Insurance covers weather and credit covers the lean months.

Do not confuse a bumper harvest with rising income. Where demand is urgent and storage is absent, more output can mean lower revenue because price falls faster than quantity grows. The top-band answer names the mechanism: perishability plus cobweb response turns abundance into loss.
bullets: Perishability and weak logistics force distress sales.
High prices today plant the glut of tomorrow.
Storage, processing and contracts smooth the cobweb.

lessons.title: Industry and Industrialization
lessons.objective: Explain industrial location and localisation, compare industrialisation strategies, and describe the role of industry, firm size and business finance.

content.heading: Industry and industrialisation
paragraphs: A cement plant sits beside a limestone deposit while a bakery sits in the city, because each location follows the cost of moving inputs and products.

content.heading: Location and localisation of industry
paragraphs: A cement factory near limestone and a bottling plant near its market choose different sites for the same reason: transport cost.

Location factors include raw materials, market, power, water, transport, labour, capital, government incentives and climate. A weight-losing industry locates near its raw material, while a weight-gaining or bulky product locates near its market. Footloose industries, such as software or tailoring, face no strong pull either way.

Localisation is the concentration of firms of one industry in a place, such as the textile firms of Kano or the oil services in Port Harcourt. It brings shared labour, suppliers and infrastructure, but also congestion, higher rents and pollution. Establishing industries in rural areas reduces rural-urban migration.
bullets: Location: raw materials, market, power, transport, labour.
Weight-losing near inputs; weight-gaining near market.
Localisation: shared gains, congestion costs.
content.takeaway: Firms locate where the total cost of moving inputs and output is lowest.

check.question: The establishment of industries in rural areas will help to reduce ______.
check.why: Rural industries create local jobs, so fewer young people need to leave the village for the city.

visual.caption: Weight-losing industries sit near inputs; weight-gaining industries sit near markets.

rows.left: The input is bulky to move
rows.right: The output is bulky to move

content.heading: Industrialisation strategies and problems
paragraphs: Nigeria tried to make what it used to import, but factories still import their machines and spare parts. Industrial strategy decides how far that works.
Import substitution protects local producers with tariffs and quotas, but it can shelter inefficient firms. Export promotion pushes firms to compete abroad and earn foreign exchange.

Other choices include small-scale and rural industries, industrial estates and privatisation. Nigeria's early plans favoured import substitution, while later policy added privatisation and support for small firms.

Industry in Nigeria faces unreliable power, poor roads and ports, scarce and costly credit, imported technology, weak management, counterfeit imports and policy inconsistency. Providing efficient infrastructure is therefore central to industrial development, because no factory can compete while it runs on generators.
bullets: Import substitution versus export promotion.
Small-scale and rural industry.
Problems: power, infrastructure, credit, technology.
content.takeaway: Protection can start an industry, but infrastructure and competition decide whether it survives.

check.question: In Nigeria, industrial development can be enhanced by ______.
options: ensuring stable prices for manufactured goods
reducing government expenditure on imported goods
check.why: Reliable power, roads and ports lower production and distribution costs, which is the base every other industrial policy needs.

content.heading: Industry, firm size and business finance
paragraphs: A mechanic's workshop and a cement plant are both firms, but they differ in size, funding and management.

Industry contributes to development by creating jobs, diversifying exports, adding value to raw materials, earning foreign exchange and generating tax revenue. It also trains workers and spreads technology to other sectors. Small firms are often sole proprietorships, while large firms take the limited-liability company form.

What sizes a firm? Market width, cash, tech, management, policy and risk. Finance runs from owners' pockets to bonds and capital markets; big names borrow cheaply, small ones scrape by on savings and microfinance.
bullets: Industry: jobs, diversification, value added, exports.
Firm size: market, capital, technology, management.
Finance: equity, retained profit, loans, bonds.
content.takeaway: Industry deepens the economy when it adds value rather than only assembling imports.

check.question: A firm that wants to expand without borrowing can use ______.
check.why: Retained profit is the firm's own past earnings, so using it avoids interest and keeps ownership unchanged.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Location is where one firm sits; localisation is many firms of one industry clustering in the same place.

content.problem: A plant can locate near its raw material or near its market. Moving inputs costs N50 per tonne, moving output costs N80 per tonne, and two tonnes of input make one tonne of output. Which site is cheaper?

steps.reason: The firm must move the finished output to the market.
steps.result: Output transport = N80 per tonne of product.
steps.predictPrompt: Now compare with moving the inputs.

steps.reason: Two tonnes of input are needed for each tonne of output.
steps.result: Input transport = 2 × N50 = N100 per tonne of product.
steps.predictPrompt: What information do you compare before deciding?

steps.reason: The cheaper site is the one with the lower total transport cost.
steps.result: The raw-material site is cheaper by N20 per tonne, so the firm locates near the deposit.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.question: Explain two reasons Nigerian industry remains weak despite decades of protection, and one policy that would strengthen it.
hints: Protection can shelter inefficient firms from competition.
Power, transport and credit raise costs and discourage investment.
A strong answer links the policy to costs or competition, not just to more spending.

content.heading: Go deeper: How transport costs actually decide a site
paragraphs: A firm compares the cost of moving inputs in and output out. If two tonnes of bulky limestone yield one tonne of cement, shifting the limestone is dearer than shifting the cement, so the plant moves to the deposit, while half a tonne of input that becomes one tonne of bulky foam pulls the firm toward the buyer. The rule is arithmetic: multiply weight by distance by rate in each direction.

Ports complicate the arithmetic. An importer whose materials arrive by sea may locate near the port even when the market lies inland, because the first leg by ship is cheap and the last leg by road is costly. A bottler who ships water in glass must move toward thirsty cities, since bottles are heavy, fragile and cheap relative to freight.

Some pulls are invisible in the freight bill. Steady power, a skilled labour pool, water for processing, land at a tolerable rent and prompt clearance of goods can save more than a short haul. Incentives that lower rent or tax shift the calculation, while unreliable power that forces hours of generator running erases the advantage of a fine address.

The edge case is the footloose firm. Tailoring, software repair or phone assembly moves little weight, so sites turn on talent, connectivity and customers rather than tonnage. Read the question for what is heavy to move, because where nothing is heavy, neither the mine nor the market should attract the firm.
bullets: Multiply weight by distance by rate in both directions.
Fragile or bulky output pulls toward the market.
Power, labour and ports can override freight alone.

content.heading: Go deeper: Import substitution, export promotion and the stages between them
paragraphs: Import substitution begins by closing the door to the foreign rival. Tariffs, quotas or a banned list give a young firm a home market in which to learn. The mechanism is the infant-industry argument: costs fall as cumulative output rises and workers master the process, so temporary shelter buys experience the market would otherwise deny.

Shelter without graduation breeds the failure the argument warns against. A firm that never faces a rival keeps costs high, quality low and managers comfortable, while the tariff taxes every user of its output. Protection that lasts without standards, time limits or performance tests therefore protects inefficiency rather than industry.

Export promotion reverses the test. Instead of shielding the firm from the world, the state pushes it into the world, where only competitive cost and acceptable quality survive. Exporters earn foreign exchange, absorb spare capacity and meet standards that discipline management, but the strategy demands ports, power, standards bodies and market intelligence that protection alone cannot supply.

Nigeria illustrates both stages. Early industrial policy favoured substitution because manufactured imports soaked up foreign exchange, yet downstream firms still imported machines, chemicals and spare parts. Later emphasis added privatisation and care for small firms, but the gap between protected assembly and genuine competitiveness remained, so the sound answer links strategy to constraint: protect only while learning, then expose to competition.
bullets: Protection buys learning; competition tests the learning.
Permanent shelter protects inefficiency, not industry.
Export promotion requires logistics and standards, not slogans.

content.heading: Go deeper: Internal growth, merger and takeover compared
paragraphs: Growth has three roads. A firm grows internally by reinvesting profit into a new line, a new shop or fuller use of existing plant. The road is gradual, keeps control in the same hands and matches expansion to the cash the business itself generates.

External growth buys speed. In a merger two firms agree to join as equals, pooling assets, brands and bosses so the combined firm acts faster than either could alone. In a takeover one firm acquires effective control of another, whether by negotiated purchase or by buying shares on the market.

Motives overlap. Firms combine to secure materials, share a distribution network, spread research costs or block a rival from buying the target, with horizontal combinations joining direct rivals, vertical combinations joining successive stages, and conglomerates joining unrelated trades to spread risk. Savings are real only if duplicated offices close, and diversification helps only if managers understand the new trade.

The examination test is control and stage. Ask who decided to combine and at which stage the partner sits. A merger between two cement makers is horizontal and a cement maker buying a quarry is backward vertical, while reinvestment of retained profit is internal growth, never a merger.
bullets: Internal growth is gradual and retains control.
Merger is mutual; takeover is control by one firm.
Stage decides horizontal versus vertical.

lessons.title: Natural Resources and the Nigerian Economy
lessons.objective: Trace Nigeria's major natural resources, distinguish upstream from downstream oil, explain oil and non-oil contributions and linkage effects, and assess the roles of NNPC, OPEC and the environmental challenges of exploitation.

content.heading: Natural resources in Nigeria
paragraphs: Nigeria earns most of its foreign exchange from crude oil, but gold, tin, limestone and timber also come from its land and forests.

content.heading: Major resources and the oil sector
paragraphs: A tanker loads crude at Bonny while a quarry in Kogi supplies limestone to a cement plant. Both are natural resources, but they enter the economy differently.

Nigeria's major resources include petroleum and natural gas, coal, tin and columbite, limestone, gold, iron ore and timber. Petroleum dominates exports and government revenue, while the others support construction, manufacturing and local livelihoods. Their development has depended on foreign capital and technology since colonial times.

The oil sector divides into upstream and downstream. Upstream covers exploration, drilling and extraction of crude oil and gas; downstream covers refining, distribution, marketing and petrochemicals. Most of Nigeria's crude is exported and its refined products imported because refinery capacity is weak.
bullets: Resources: oil, gas, coal, tin, limestone, gold, timber.
Upstream: exploration and extraction.
Downstream: refining, distribution, marketing.
content.takeaway: Upstream finds and lifts the oil; downstream turns it into products people buy.

check.question: The main activity in the upstream oil sector in Nigeria is ______.
check.why: Upstream work happens at the wellhead, where oil and gas are explored, drilled and extracted before refining or sale.

visual.caption: Upstream lifts crude; downstream refines and sells it.

rows.left: Oil well in the Niger Delta

content.heading: Oil, the non-oil sector and linkage effects
paragraphs: Oil pays most of the budget, but it employs few people directly. Agriculture and services employ far more, which is why the non-oil sector still matters.

Oil contributes foreign exchange, government revenue and energy, while the non-oil sector contributes employment, food, manufactured goods and most GDP. Over-dependence on oil exposes the economy to price shocks and can cause Dutch disease, where oil exports raise the exchange rate and make other exports uncompetitive.

Linkage effects are the connections through which one sector pulls others along. Backward linkages buy inputs from local suppliers; forward linkages process the output; consumption linkages spend oil wages on local goods; fiscal linkages spend oil revenue on public investment. Weak linkages explain why oil wealth has not transformed Nigerian industry.
bullets: Oil: foreign exchange, revenue, energy.
Non-oil: jobs, food, output.
Linkages: backward, forward, consumption, fiscal.
content.takeaway: Oil pays the government, but only strong linkages make it develop the rest of the economy.

check.question: A backward linkage in the oil sector refers to ______.
options: oil firms buying inputs from local suppliers
exporting crude oil to foreign buyers
check.why: A backward linkage looks upstream to suppliers, so it is the demand oil firms create for local inputs and services.

content.heading: NNPC, OPEC and the challenges of exploitation
paragraphs: Niger Delta communities live with spilled oil and flared gas while the revenue leaves by pipeline and tanker. That contrast is the resource curse in everyday form.

The Nigerian National Petroleum Company manages state interests in exploration, production, refining and marketing, while OPEC coordinates member quotas and prices. Since 2021 the NNPC is a limited-liability company, while the NUPRC and NMDPRA regulate upstream and downstream. OPEC quotas can limit Nigeria's output, and price decisions affect its revenue.

Challenges include oil spills and gas flaring, pipeline vandalism and theft, pollution of farmland and water, weak enforcement, unstable global prices and the neglect of other sectors. Clean-up, stricter environmental rules, community agreements, diversified exports and saved oil revenue reduce the damage.
bullets: NNPC: state oil operations. OPEC: quotas and prices.
Challenges: spills, flaring, theft, pollution.
Responses: clean-up, regulation, diversification, savings.
content.takeaway: Natural resources build an economy only when the revenue and the environment are both managed.

check.question: Gas flaring is best described as ______.
options: burning associated gas during oil production
check.why: Gas flaring burns the gas that comes up with crude oil when it cannot be captured, sold or reinjected.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Upstream is finding and extracting; downstream is refining and selling. Refining is never upstream.

content.problem: A barrel of crude sells for $80. Production costs $20 per barrel and government takes 60 per cent of the profit. Find the profit per barrel and the government's revenue per barrel.

steps.reason: Profit is the selling price minus the production cost.
steps.predictPrompt: What is 60 per cent of $60?

steps.reason: The government's share is 60 per cent of the profit.
