content.question: Explain how weak linkages reduce the development effect of Nigeria's oil wealth, and name one policy that would strengthen them.
hints: Weak backward linkages mean oil firms import their equipment and services.
Weak forward linkages mean crude is exported rather than refined or used in local manufacturing.
A policy could require local content, fund refining or invest oil revenue in infrastructure and skills.

content.heading: Go deeper: Dutch disease and why oil can shrink other exports
paragraphs: An oil boom raises earnings, government spending and wages. The spending effect runs first through the economy: more naira chasing the same food, housing and services bids up their prices. Workers leave farms and factories for construction and public jobs because those pay more.

The resource-movement effect runs alongside it. Labour and capital shift toward the booming sector and the non-tradable activities it feeds, starving the tradable farm and factory sectors of workers. A cocoa farmer or textile maker loses hands to a higher wage, keeps the old world price, and is squeezed from both sides.

Foreign exchange inflow sharpens the squeeze. When dollars from crude are converted into naira, the naira firms, so a bag of cocoa or a crate of groundnuts earns fewer naira at the same world price. Costs set in naira stay high while earnings set in dollars shrink, so the exporter is punished precisely when the nation celebrates its oil receipts.

The lesson is temporary relief, not permanent cure. Saving oil revenue, holding a stabilisation fund, and investing in power, transport and skills raise the competing sectors rather than suppress the exchange rate by wishful thinking. Examinations test the direction: oil raises government revenue while weakening other exports.
bullets: Spending bids up costs for other exporters.
A firmer exchange rate cuts export earnings in naira.
Saving and investing in supply are the lasting remedy.

content.heading: Go deeper: Local content and the hard arithmetic of linkages
paragraphs: A backward linkage is the demand an oil firm creates for local inputs. It is strong only when a supplier can meet the oil firm's specification at a competitive cost and on time. Equipment that must survive heat, pressure and salt, delivered without fail, sets a standard many new Nigerian firms cannot yet meet.

Forward linkages process the crude after extraction. Refining, petrochemicals, gas processing and power generation turn a raw export into higher-value products consumed at home. Each step needs capital, technology, steady feedstock and buyers, so where refineries run poorly or gas is flared, the forward chain breaks.

Consumption and fiscal linkages leak for similar reasons. Oil wages spent on imported goods, and oil revenue spent on imported project inputs, create demand abroad rather than at home. Local content rules and supplier development funds try to retain the spending, but they raise costs if the local source is weak.

For examinations, place each linkage by position. Buying pipes locally is backward, refining is forward, spending wages at home is consumption, and spending revenue on schools is fiscal. A policy strengthens linkages only when it builds a supplier able to compete after the incentive ends, so ask who must now be able to deliver and the answer separates a real linkage from a rent.
bullets: Backward means local supply that meets oil specifications.
Forward means refining and processing of the crude.
Local content without capability raises cost without linkages.

content.heading: Go deeper: Who regulates what after the NNPC reform
paragraphs: The Nigerian National Petroleum Company once combined the roles of owner, operator and adviser to the state. That combination created a conflict: the referee that should fine the polluter was also earning from the pollution. Under the Petroleum Industry Act, the NNPC is now a limited-liability company that operates like a commercial firm, while regulation was separated.

Separation divides the field. The upstream regulator supervises exploration, drilling and production, including licences, metering and flaring rules, while the downstream regulator supervises refining, distribution, marketing and petrochemicals, including product quality and pipeline access. The NNPC competes in that regulated market and pays taxes and royalties rather than answering to itself.

OPEC still sits above the national regulators. Member quotas can cap how much Nigeria may lift, and market prices decide what each barrel earns regardless of domestic plans. A regulator who grants a licence therefore does not guarantee revenue, because the quota and the price may move against the nation.

Host communities add a fourth pressure. Clean-up duties, trust funds and agreed development obligations try to reconcile the Niger Delta burden of spills and flares with the national benefit of the revenue. Where those obligations are honoured, regulation gains local legitimacy; where they are evaded, vandalism and theft replace consent.
bullets: NNPC operates commercially; it does not regulate itself.
Upstream and downstream regulators split the field.
OPEC quotas and world prices limit national revenue.

lessons.title: Business Organisations
lessons.objective: Compare private business forms on ownership, liability and finance, assess public enterprises and privatisation, and explain business funding, firm size and integration.

content.heading: Business organisations
paragraphs: A tailor registers his shop as a business name while two friends form a limited liability company. The form they choose decides who is liable and how much capital they can raise.

content.heading: Private enterprises
paragraphs: A sole proprietorship has one owner and unlimited liability. A partnership has two to twenty persons who share capital and profits, but also bear unlimited liability.

A private limited company has restricted shares and limited liability; a public limited company can trade its shares publicly and raise far more capital. A co-operative is owned and controlled by its members, who are usually also its customers, on a one-member-one-vote basis.
Incorporation makes the company a separate legal person, so it owns assets, signs contracts and continues when shareholders change. Unincorporated businesses lack that perpetual succession.
bullets: Sole trader: one owner, unlimited liability.
Partnership: two to twenty partners, unlimited liability.
Companies: limited liability, perpetual succession.
content.takeaway: The business form decides who bears the risk and how much capital can be raised.

check.question: The maximum number of persons allowed in an ordinary partnership under Nigerian law is ______.
check.why: An ordinary partnership is capped at twenty persons; anything larger must incorporate as a company.

visual.caption: Incorporation separates the business from its owners.

content.heading: Public enterprises, privatisation and commercialisation
paragraphs: A state water board serves the public but runs at a loss and depends on subsidy. Public enterprises are set up for services markets may not provide, yet they often become a burden.

Public enterprises are owned by government and include public corporations, parastatals and government companies. They aim to provide essential services, control strategic sectors, create employment and correct market failure. Their problems include political interference, weak accountability, overstaffing, corruption, poor maintenance and losses covered by subsidy.

Privatisation transfers ownership of a public enterprise to private investors, while commercialisation keeps government ownership but makes the enterprise charge cost-reflective prices and run commercially. Privatisation can raise efficiency and revenue but may cause job losses and higher prices; commercialisation keeps public control but may still lack competition.
bullets: Public enterprises: government-owned, service motive.
Problems: politics, overstaffing, losses.
Privatisation sells; commercialisation makes commercial.
content.takeaway: Ownership can change faster than the incentives and competition that make an enterprise efficient.

check.question: Privatisation differs from commercialisation because privatisation ______.
options: only raises the price of services
check.why: Privatisation changes who owns the enterprise, while commercialisation keeps public ownership and changes how it is run.

content.heading: Funding, management and the size of firms
paragraphs: A bakery that buys a flour mill is growing backwards, while one that buys a rival bakery is growing sideways. Both change the size and scope of the firm.

Firms need finance for fixed capital, working capital and expansion. Sources include owners' equity, retained profits, bank loans, trade credit, leasing, bonds and the capital market; small firms rely on savings, family loans and microfinance, while large firms borrow more cheaply.

The size of a firm depends on market size, capital, technology, management skill, risk and government policy. Growth can be internal, through reinvestment, or external, through merger and takeover. Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage, vertical integration joins firms at different stages to enjoy economies of large-scale production, and a conglomerate joins unrelated businesses.
bullets: Finance: equity, retained profit, loans, bonds.
Size: market, capital, technology, management.
Integration: horizontal, vertical, conglomerate.
content.takeaway: A firm grows when its market and management can carry more capital and technology.

check.question: Firms embark on vertical integration in order to ______.
options: take over markets formerly controlled by other firms
prevent other firms from entering the market
check.why: Vertical integration joins stages of production or distribution, so one firm internalises the chain and captures its economies.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Incorporation is the dividing line. A company is a separate legal person; a sole trader is not.

content.problem: Two friends need N50 million and want to limit their personal risk. Which business form should they choose, and why not a partnership?

steps.reason: A partnership leaves owners personally liable for business debts.
steps.result: A partnership does not cap personal risk.
steps.predictPrompt: Which form limits liability and can raise outside capital?

steps.reason: A limited liability company is a separate legal person and can issue shares.
steps.result: A private limited company fits, and it can later become public to raise more capital.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you verify this answer?

steps.reason: Incorporation brings registration, disclosure and compliance costs.
steps.result: They accept formalities in exchange for limited liability and easier capital raising.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.question: Why might a co-operative charge members lower prices than a private shop selling the same goods?
hints: A co-operative is owned by its members, not by outside shareholders seeking maximum profit.
Any surplus is returned to members, so the effective price is lower.
A strong answer links ownership and surplus distribution to the price members pay.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why a company can outlive its founders
paragraphs: Incorporation creates a legal person separate from its members. The company owns land and equipment, signs contracts, opens bank accounts and can sue or be sued in its own name. An asset bought by the company belongs to the company, so a shareholder who leaves does not take a machine with them.

Perpetual succession follows from that separateness. Shares pass from one holder to another while the company itself persists, like a market that outlives its traders. A sole proprietorship dies with the proprietor unless assets are rebuilt, and a partnership dissolves when a partner leaves unless the deed says otherwise.

Limited liability is the shadow of separateness. A shareholder risks only the value of shares bought, while the company's debts rest on company assets. The shield has edges because directors who trade fraudulently or use the company as a sham may still face personal liability, and courts unwrap the veil where the form is used to deceive.

The discrimination is registration and registration alone. A tailor who registers a business name has not incorporated and remains personally liable. A tailor who registers a private limited company has created a separate person, however small the workshop, so if the form was not incorporated the owner is the firm, and if yes the firm is the person.
bullets: Incorporation creates a separate legal person.
Perpetual succession lets the firm outlive members.
Limited liability has edges for fraud and sham use.

content.heading: Go deeper: Commercialisation without privatisation and the half-owned trap
paragraphs: Commercialisation keeps the state as owner but changes the rules of running. The enterprise must charge prices that cover costs, keep proper accounts, appoint managers for performance, and earn a return rather than spend a subvention. A water board that meters users and bills for maintenance is commercialised, even though the ministry still holds the shares.

The half-owned trap appears when the rules change but the discipline does not. Politicians hold prices below cost before elections, treasury covers the gap with subsidies, managers answer to ministers rather than customers, and no competitor punishes waste. The enterprise then bears the label commercial while the soft budget constraint of the past persists.

Privatisation goes further by transferring ownership to private investors who bear the loss if the firm fails. The transfer alone does not manufacture efficiency, so a monopoly sold without regulation keeps its power to overcharge and a firm sold without a credible tariff keeps its claim on the treasury. Sound sequencing therefore regulates, restructures debts, allows competition, then sells.

For examinations, separate owner, price and discipline. If ownership moves, the reform is privatisation, if only the price and accounts change it is commercialisation, and if neither moves the reform is a press statement. Neither reform saves an enterprise whose costs nobody is allowed to control.
bullets: Commercialisation changes price and discipline, not owner.
Privatisation transfers ownership and risk to investors.
Soft budgets defeat either reform without competition.

content.heading: Go deeper: Horizontal, vertical and conglomerate growth on the ground
paragraphs: Take a bakery that buys a rival bakery across town. The addition operates at the same stage, selling the same loaves to the same kind of customer, so the combination is horizontal. The gain is market share, a shared oven timetable and a single brand where two competed.

Let the same bakery buy a flour mill or a fleet of delivery vans. The new asset sits at an earlier or later stage of the same chain, so the combination is vertical. Backward integration secures flour quality and supply and forward integration secures delivery and sales outlets, so the firm internalises a market that once charged a margin.

A conglomerate joins unrelated trades under one holding company: flour, furniture and haulage with no common input or customer. The motive is risk spreading, since cement and transport rarely fall together, and the use of surplus cash where the home trade offers no outlet. Unrelated assets help only when headquarters can judge each trade without favouring its own.

Classify by stage before you classify by size. Two brewers joining is horizontal, a brewer buying barley farms is backward vertical, a brewer buying bars is forward vertical, and a brewer buying a cement firm is a conglomerate. Internal growth by reinvesting profit is none of these, and the pattern reveals itself in who supplies whom and who competes with whom.
bullets: Horizontal joins rivals at the same stage.
Vertical joins successive stages of one chain.
Conglomerates join unrelated trades for risk spreading.

lessons.title: Population, Census and the Labour Force
lessons.objective: Distinguish over-, under- and optimum population, interpret population structure and dependency, and assess the census and population policy in Nigeria.

content.heading: Population
paragraphs: Nigeria's population grows faster than its farms and factories, so each new job must support more people. Whether that is a problem depends on the size of the population relative to resources.

content.heading: Size, growth and population theory
paragraphs: Malthus argued that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so checks such as famine and disease keep it in line. His prediction failed because technology raised food output, but his warning still applies where growth outruns resources.

Over-population means more people than available resources can support at a decent standard; under-population means too few people to use resources fully; optimum population maximises income per head. Population growth comes from births and immigration minus deaths and emigration.
The size and growth of a population depend on birth rates, death rates and migration, and on income, education, health care and cultural attitudes to family size.
bullets: Malthus: population outruns food.
Over-, under- and optimum population.
Growth = births + immigration − deaths − emigration.
content.takeaway: Population is a problem only in relation to the resources and jobs available.

check.question: A population is described as optimum when it ______.
options: is the largest the country can hold
check.why: Optimum population is the size that gives the highest income per person, not the largest population a country can hold.

visual.caption: Over-population presses on resources; under-population leaves them idle.

rows.right: Too few people to use resources
Immigration and incentives to raise births

content.heading: Structure, distribution and the labour force
paragraphs: A country with many children needs schools now and jobs later, while one with many elderly people needs clinics and pensions. Age structure decides those needs.

Population structure covers age, sex, occupation, education and location. The working population, or labour force, is the number of people able and willing to work; the dependency ratio divides dependants by the working-age population.

Distribution is uneven: cities attract migrants with jobs and services, while rural areas lose young people. Occupational distribution is mainly influenced by economic factors such as wages, skills and job availability. A youthful population needs schools and jobs, while an ageing one needs health and pension spending, and migration is pushed by low wages, insecurity and unemployment and pulled by jobs and services.
bullets: Structure: age, sex, occupation, location.
Dependency ratio = dependants ÷ working-age population.
Migration: push and pull factors.
content.takeaway: Age structure tells a government what to build now and what to fund later.

check.question: The number of people who are qualified to work and who offer themselves for employment is called the ______.
check.why: The working population or labour force counts those able and willing to work, not everyone of working age.

content.heading: Census, growth and population policy
paragraphs: A census counts every person, but Nigeria's figures have been disputed because some areas fear undercounting and others inflate their numbers.

A census is important for economic planning, revenue allocation, constituency delimitation and labour-force estimates. Its problems include cost, illiteracy, difficult terrain, religious and ethnic sensitivity, poor logistics and political manipulation.

Population policy aims to influence size, growth and distribution through family planning, girls' education, health care, job creation and migration management. In Nigeria, rapid growth with high youth dependency means schools, clinics and jobs must expand faster than the population, or development gains are absorbed by more people.
bullets: Census: planning, revenue, constituencies.
Problems: cost, terrain, politics, logistics.
Policy: family planning, education, health, jobs.
content.takeaway: A census is only useful when the data are trusted and actually used for planning.

check.question: A well-conducted census is important for ______.
options: providing economic opportunities in rural areas
check.why: Census figures tell planners how many schools, clinics, roads and jobs are needed where, which is the core of economic planning.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Optimum population is not the largest possible population. It is the size that maximises income per head.

content.problem: A country has 120 million people: 45 million under 15, 5 million over 64, and a labour force of 50 million. Find the working-age population, the dependency ratio and the participation rate.

steps.reason: Subtract the dependent age groups from the total.
steps.predictPrompt: Which groups count as dependants?

steps.reason: Dependants are the under-15 and over-64 groups: 45 + 5 = 50 million.
steps.predictPrompt: In your own words, why does this step come before the next one?

steps.reason: The labour force is those working or actively seeking work, not everyone of working age.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.question: Explain why rapid population growth can help or hurt economic development, and name one policy that would make the difference.
hints: A large young population can be a workforce and a market if jobs and skills exist.
It becomes a burden when schools, clinics and jobs cannot keep pace.
Education, health care and job creation turn growth into a dividend.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the dependency ratio moves in waves, not in straight lines
paragraphs: Dependency ratios move in waves. When births are high and deaths fall, the child share rises fast and the ratio climbs, because schools and clinics must serve a crowd while few adults are available to pay. As that large cohort ages, the working-age share swells and the ratio falls.

The falling phase is the only window for a demographic dividend. A larger workforce can produce more, save more and finance more per head, but only if the workers are healthy, skilled and employed. Youthful energy does not employ itself, so where jobs, power and training lag, the dividend becomes a queue of unemployed graduates and informal traders.

Youth and old-age dependence pull the budget in opposite directions. Youth dependence demands classrooms, teachers, vaccines and maternity care now, while old-age dependence demands pensions, hospitals and geriatric care later. A country that neglects education while planning pensions has mismatched its spending to its wave.

Do not equate working age with working. The labour force counts only those able, willing and actually seeking work, so students, the ill and discouraged jobseekers of working age sit outside it. A falling age-based ratio can therefore coexist with a rising labour-based burden when participation is low.
bullets: Cohorts move the ratio down then up again.
The dividend needs jobs, health and skills.
Working age is not the same as the labour force.

content.heading: Go deeper: Undercount, overcount and the politics of the census
paragraphs: A census count is also a claim on money and power. Where revenue allocation and legislative seats follow population, a state, local government or community has reason to inflate its number, and rivals have reason to cry fraud. Conversely, groups that fear taxation or conscription may hide their members, and mistrust precedes the counting, so no careful method will be accepted if the incentives to manipulate remain.

Distrust deepens where the ground resists counting. Difficult terrain, seasonal migration, nomadic movement, insecure areas and dense informal settlements all leave enumerators guessing at doors that cannot be marked. Illiteracy turns a form into a barrier, and religious or ethnic sensitivity turns a question about origin into a dispute.

Technique can narrow the gap but cannot remove it. Call-backs, satellite maps of settlements, post-enumeration surveys, administrative records and satellite imagery all cross-check the headcount. Yet each fixes a definition that excludes someone: a person counted at home while living in the city counts double for two plans or none.

The examination distinction is between importance and accuracy. A census matters for planning, revenue, seats and labour estimates precisely because those claims are so valuable. That value is also the reason the figures are fought over, so a well-conducted census is important not because numbers are automatically true, but because no fair allocation is possible without a defensible count.
bullets: Revenue and seats give reasons to inflate figures.
Terrain, mobility and sensitivity defeat casual counting.
Importance is not the same as accuracy.

content.heading: Go deeper: Push, pull and the gendered edge of migration
paragraphs: Migrants move when the difference between staying and going justifies the cost. Push factors drive from the origin in the form of low wages, unemployment, drought and insecurity, while pull factors beckon at the destination as jobs, higher wages, schools, hospitals and safety. Either side alone rarely moves a household.

Movement is selective, not random. Young adults able to walk, pay transport and endure risk move first, leaving the village older and shorter of strong hands. Men often move first for wage work while women sustain farms and children, or women move for domestic and market trade while men keep the land.

Remittances and return complete the circuit. Money sent home builds houses, funds school fees and smooths lean seasons, altering consumption in villages movers never intended to leave. Return, when jobs dry or the migrant retires, brings skills or imports city habits that unsettle local custom, so rural-urban movement is thus a circulation, not a single departure.

Policy must weigh origin and destination together. Rural roads and power hold some households, but a city that cannot house its newcomers converts a pull into a slum. Girls' education, portable health care and skills that travel with the worker improve the terms on both sides, so the trap is to name one factor alone rather than pair the push with the pull.
bullets: Push forces the move; pull receives the mover.
Migrants are selected by age, sex and skill.
Remittances and return link origin to destination.
